U.S. equity futures bounced on Sunday, as a shortened week on Wall Street got underway after all three major averages ended Friday in correction territory.

Futures tied to the Dow Jones Industrial Average gained 353 points, or 0.7%. S&P 500 futures added 1.3%, and Nasdaq-100 futures rose 2.3%.

Last week, the major indexes tumbled as worries about the artificial intelligence trade continued to spook investors, despite Anthropic's record debut on Thursday.

By the end of the rout last week — which was the worst weekly decline for the Nasdaq Composite and Dow in more than six years, and the largest for the S&P 500 since April 2025 — all three of the major averages were in correction territory, and the Nasdaq turned negative for the year.

The Nasdaq-100 index ended Friday in bear market territory on an intraday basis, but was just shy of that mark based on the decline from its closing high on Oct. 6.

Investors this week will get a breather, no matter what price action looks like. Markets are closed on Thursday for the Thanksgiving holiday, and Friday's session will be shortened with the closing bell set to ring at 1:00 p.m.

Common medications may secretly rewire your gut, with effects lasting for years

- Date:

- November 22, 2026

- Source:

- Estonian Research Council

- Summary:

- Medications taken years or even long ago may leave lasting changes in your gut microbiome, according to a study of more than 2,500 people. Researchers discovered that common drugs, including antidepressants, blood pressure medications, and anxiety treatments, can leave microbial âfingerprintsâ long after patients stop taking them. Surprisingly, some anxiety medications had effects comparable to broad-spectrum antibiotics.

- Share:

Medications you stopped taking years ago may still be influencing the bacteria living in your gut. A large study from the University of Tartu Institute of Genomics has found that many commonly prescribed drugs leave lasting changes in the gut microbiome, even long after people stop using them.

The gut microbiome is the vast community of bacteria and other microorganisms that inhabit the digestive tract. These microbes play important roles in digestion, immune function, and overall health. While antibiotics are well known for disrupting gut bacteria, the new findings suggest that many other medications can also have effects that persist for years.

To investigate these connections, researchers examined stool samples and prescription histories from more than 2,500 participants in the Estonian Biobank's Estonian Microbiome cohort. They discovered that most of the medications studied were associated with changes in gut bacteria. Even more surprisingly, a substantial number left detectable microbial "fingerprints" years after patients had stopped taking them.

Common Medications Leave Lasting Changes in Gut Bacteria

The findings extend far beyond antibiotics. Antidepressants, beta-blockers, proton pump inhibitors, and benzodiazepines were all linked to differences in the gut microbiome.

These medications are widely used to treat everyday health conditions. Beta-blockers are commonly prescribed for high blood pressure and certain heart conditions, while proton pump inhibitors reduce stomach acid and are frequently used to treat acid reflux. Benzodiazepines are often prescribed for anxiety, and antidepressants help manage depression and other mental health conditions.

"Most microbiome studies only consider current medications, but our results show that past drug use can be just as important as it is a surprisingly strong factor in explaining individual microbiome differences," said Dr. Oliver Aasmets, lead author.

This discovery suggests that looking only at the medications someone currently takes may overlook an important part of their gut health history. Previous prescriptions could help explain why the composition of gut bacteria differs so much from one person to another.

Anxiety Medications Show Effects Comparable to Antibiotics

One of the most striking findings involved benzodiazepines, a class of medications commonly used to treat anxiety.

Researchers found that these drugs were associated with changes in the gut microbiome comparable to those seen with broad-spectrum antibiotics. These antibiotics target a wide variety of bacteria and are known to substantially alter the microbial communities living in the digestive system.

The researchers also discovered that medications within the same drug class did not necessarily produce the same effects. For example, diazepam and alprazolam are both benzodiazepines used to treat similar conditions, yet they appeared to differ in how strongly they disrupted gut bacteria.

This suggests that the effects of medication on the microbiome may depend not only on the type of drug being taken, but also on the specific medication.

Gut Bacteria Can Change When Medications Are Started or Stopped

To investigate whether medications were actually contributing to these microbial changes, researchers collected additional stool samples from a smaller group of participants.

By examining how the microbiome changed when people started or stopped certain medications, the team identified predictable shifts in gut bacteria. These findings provided additional evidence that the drugs themselves were contributing to the changes, rather than simply being associated with differences already present in patients.

Although the number of participants in this follow-up analysis was relatively small, the researchers were able to verify lasting effects associated with several drug categories. These included proton pump inhibitors, selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, and certain antibiotics, including combinations of penicillins and macrolides.

Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, often called SSRIs, are a widely prescribed type of antidepressant. Macrolides are a class of antibiotics used to treat various bacterial infections.

Why Your Medication History May Matter More Than Previously Thought

The findings point to an important consideration for researchers studying the relationship between gut bacteria and disease. Differences in the microbiome may reflect not only a person's current health and medication use, but also treatments received years earlier.

If previous medications are not taken into account, scientists could mistakenly attribute certain microbial differences to a disease or another health factor when past drug exposure may have contributed.

The results also highlight how much remains to be understood about the long-term relationship between medications and the gut microbiome. Although the study identified persistent microbial changes, these findings do not establish that such changes are necessarily harmful or that they lead to specific health problems.

"This is a comprehensive systematic evaluation of long-term medication effects on the microbiome using real-world medical health records," said Professor Elin Org, corresponding author. "We hope this encourages researchers and clinicians to factor in medication history when interpreting microbiome data."

item.title: Earth just saw the most anomalously hot day ever on record
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Clean-up failed for this item, so the body is a truncated excerpt of the original.)

Why it is here: original reporting, evidence and concrete detail

Earth just saw the most anomalously hot day ever measured on the planet. According to preliminary data from the Europe-based Copernicus Climate Change Service (C3S), Friday, November 20, 2026 was 2.12 degrees Celsius higher than the preindustrial average—or the time before human's began heating up the Earth by burning fossil fuels.

The record stems from a combination of long-term, human-driven climate change and a blockbuster El Niño that is likely the strongest in the past 1,000 years. It come as international negotiations at the COP 31 climate summit fell apart, with no global agreement on how to rein in global warming.

On supporting science journalism

If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.

There are likely to be more days with an anomaly at or above 2 degrees C as this El Niño builds to its crescendo over roughly the next month. The next several months are also likely to be record hot. "I think we will likely see more days exceeding 2 degrees C over the next couple of months (possibly through March 2027)," says Zachary Labe, a scientist at Climate Central, a climate research nonprofit. "Though I still expect this to be more a rarity than the norm when comparing every day"

It's possible 2026 will be the hottest year on record, besting 2024, though it will be close and could end in a tie. Because it takes time for the heat released by El Niño in the Pacific to affect global temperatures, 2027 will likely see the biggest heat effect and will almost certainly become the hottest year on record. Both 2026 and 2027 will be more than 1.5 degrees C above preindustrial temperatures, a level so far only ever surpassed in 2024.

Under the landmark 2015 Paris climate agreement, which came out of the COP 21 meeting, countries agreed to limit warming to "well below" 2 degrees C above preindustrial and to try to keep it under 1.5 degrees C. But the United Nations (UN) recently announced that the world will blow past the 1.5 degrees C mark, with global temperatures expected to hit 1.8 degrees C above preindustrial.

Surpassing the 2 degrees C benchmark for a day—or even a year—doesn't mean the Paris agreement limit has been permanently breached, as that considers the average temperature over many years. By that measure, the world has warmed by nearly 1.4 degrees C above preindustrial, according to the UN.

The COP31 summit—to which the U.S. did not send an official delegation—ended without an agreement for a final deal. These documents nominally provide a blueprint for countries to follow in their efforts to lower greenhouse gas emissions and adapt to the changing climate.

In a statement, outgoing Secretary General Antonio Guterres, who has been a vocal supporter of phasing out fossil fuels, noted his "profound frustration" at the summit's outcome. "Temperatures keep shattering records. Climate extremes keep intensifying. Emissions remain far too high. And every delay makes our task harder and more costly," Guterres said. "The world is now poised to exceed the globally-agreed limit of a 1.5 degree temperature rise. The window to keep that overshoot as short and shallow as possible is rapidly closing."

Type 2 diabetes linked to 53% higher Alzheimerâs risk, major review finds

- November 22, 2026

- Source:

- Summary:

- People with type 2 diabetes face a 53% higher risk of developing Alzheimerâs disease, according to a major new review of 40 studies. Researchers estimate that nearly five out of every 1,000 people with type 2 diabetes develop Alzheimerâs each year. By focusing specifically on these two conditions, the study offers a clearer understanding of a potentially serious connection between metabolic health and brain health.

A major research review led by Curtin University has found that people with type 2 diabetes face a significantly higher risk of developing Alzheimer's disease. The findings provide a clearer picture of the connection between diabetes and Alzheimer's, including how much the risk increases and how frequently new cases occur.

Researchers analyzed data from 40 studies in a systematic review and meta-analysis. They estimated that for every 1,000 people with type 2 diabetes, approximately 4.7 would develop Alzheimer's disease over the course of one year.

A separate analysis found that people with type 2 diabetes had a 53 percent higher adjusted relative risk of developing Alzheimer's compared with those without the condition.

Understanding the Link Between Diabetes and Alzheimer's

Study author Dr. Emmanuel Adewuyi, an NHMRC Investigator Fellow at the Curtin School of Population Health, explained that the findings offer a more precise understanding of Alzheimer's risk among people with type 2 diabetes.

Unlike previous research reviews that often examined multiple forms of diabetes or dementia together, this analysis concentrated specifically on type 2 diabetes and Alzheimer's disease. It also measured how frequently people with diabetes developed Alzheimer's, providing an additional perspective on the connection between the two conditions.

"While many earlier reviews combined different types of diabetes or dementia, this review focused specifically on type 2 diabetes and Alzheimer's disease and estimated how often new cases occurred," Dr. Adewuyi said.

"Relative risk tells us how two groups compare, while incidence tells us how often new cases occur: putting those numbers together gives us a clearer picture of the burden of Alzheimer's disease among people living with type 2 diabetes."

The study, "Incidence and risk of Alzheimer's disease in individuals with type 2 diabetes: a systematic review and meta-analysis," was published in Alzheimer's Research & Therapy.

item.description:

Why it is here: original reporting, useful vocabulary

New species can be discovered in all sorts of ways. In the case of Rhacophorus kurniatia, a type of Asian flying frog that’s only just been identified, it involved a trek deep into the Mekongga Mountains in Indonesia, to a secluded lake where thousands of frogs had congregated.

“We were moving up the mountain, and we came across this big pond covered in these green frogs,” Alan Hitch, one of the authors of a new study about Rhacophorus kurniatia, explained in a statement. “They were all over. You don’t really see frogs in big congregations like that. This was something super special.”

They were quickly identified as being flying frogs, from the Rhacophorus genus. The large webbed feet, for gliding between trees, were the main giveaway. Further analysis revealed something not seen in other Rhacophorus species, though: The frogs deposit their eggs in gelatinous masses hanging above or near water, rather than in the typical foamy nests.

Distinctive, pointed snouts, as well as differences in the calls made by the frogs, confirmed that this was a species that hadn’t been observed and documented before.

“The team looked at hundreds and hundreds of specimens of frogs to describe the new species,” study author Andrew Engilis Jr. said in a statement. “Sometimes species can look the same, but their behavior is different and their genetics are different—these are called cryptic species. This frog is an example of that. It looks very similar to other Rhacophorus, but its genetics and behavior show that it’s very distinctive.”

The identification of R. kurniatia is the culmination of four years of work on the Indonesian island of Sulawesi, which is close to Borneo. Expeditions carried out by the researchers led them from sea level to the highest mountain peaks—with the new flying frog species discovered some 6,100 feet above sea level.

And there’s a bittersweet reason for the naming: The flying frog’s scientific name was chosen as a mark of respect for renowned herpetologist Hellen Kurniati, who died in 2024. She was one of the leading researchers studying amphibians and reptiles in Indonesia. She also helped to discover the new species that now shares her name.

item.description:

Why it is here: original reporting, useful vocabulary

November 22, 2026 report

JWST finds a possible black hole that grew faster than its host galaxy in the early universe

Shreejaya Karantha

Author

Gaby Clark

Scientific Editor

Robert Egan

Senior Editor

How the first massive black holes formed in the universe remains an open question in astronomy. Black holes weighing about a billion solar masses within the first billion years of the universe require extraordinary origin stories.

Now, a new multiwavelength study of a potential black hole may offer a clue. Combining spectroscopy from the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) with Hubble imaging and archival data from the Very Large Telescope's MUSE instrument, astronomers identified this black hole in MARTA 3887, a clumpy, metal-poor galaxy as seen about 12 billion years ago. This black hole appears to have a mass of about 3.3 million suns and sits in a galaxy containing roughly 145 million solar masses in stars. The discovery paper, posted to the arXiv preprint server, explains why this is unusual.

Overmassive black holes

Many recent studies have revealed early black holes that have a different relationship with their host galaxies, compared to what's seen in the nearby universe. Early black holes are too heavy compared to their host galaxies' stellar masses. This suggests the black holes in the early universe may grow quicker than the stars.

Researchers point out another factor that may affect the 'overmassive black holes' sample. Surveys can only detect black holes that are bright or fast-moving enough, so the samples have the heaviest ones for a given galaxy mass. Those giant black holes are only the tip of the iceberg. To really understand how black holes form and grow, astronomers need to look for the smaller, more typical ones too. But these are also hard to detect.

The signals from supernovae exploding into dense gas, shocks, and outflows can mimic faint black holes. In young, metal-poor galaxies, the spectral line ratios used to differentiate black hole-powered gas from star-powered gas may overlap, and extreme stars can mimic an active galactic nucleus (AGN), a galaxy powered by a massive black hole.

'Outpaced' growth

In the new study, Mirko Curti of the INAF—Astrophysics and Space Science Observatory of Bologna and colleagues used many lines of evidence rather than one to ask whether the object at the center of MARTA 3887 is an overmassive black hole.

Using the spectroscopic observations from JWST, they detected a wide hydrogen-alpha line, which revealed that the gas is moving at about 1,270 kilometers per second (790 miles per second). The signal appeared only in hydrogen, not in other kinds of lines such as those from oxygen that come from calmer gas. This pointed to a black hole rather than an ordinary outflow.

Next, they estimated the black hole's mass: roughly 3.3 million times the sun's mass. This mass estimate places it among the lower-mass black holes found by JWST. The galaxy, on the other hand, has about 145 million solar masses of stars, so the black hole is roughly 2.3% of the stellar mass.

Researchers note that this relation is "approximately 2 dex above the local relation," which means it is about 100 times higher than the relationship extrapolated from nearby galaxies. This suggests that "black-hole growth has outpaced the assembly of the observed stellar component," the team writes in the paper.

The galaxy itself is compact and clumpy and is low in heavy elements, about 10% of the sun's level, which is typical of a young galaxy. It is forming stars fast, roughly five to nine solar masses of new stars per year, mostly in a recent burst.

Growth tracking

The researchers then explored how the 'outpacing' could have happened. They built simple growth trackers assuming one black hole grows steadily from a seed, with no mergers, at a constant feeding rate. Each track was set to end at the measured mass at the time they observed the galaxy.

They found that if black hole growth began very early, when the universe was about 0.1 billion years old, the seeds with masses of 100, 10,000, and 100,000 suns would need to feed at about 34%, 19%, and 11% of the maximum rate. If growth began only with the recent star-formation burst, a 100-solar-mass seed would need to feed at about 570% of the maximum rate, which is extreme. This means a small black-hole seed that began its growth later would require strongly super-Eddington growth, while a more massive initial seed could grow more slowly.

The team is careful to note that this galaxy 'possibly' hosts a black hole. An interacting supernova or a compact and thick outflow could still mimic the signal, though these explanations are less likely. They cannot rule out these scenarios from data gathered during a single observation.

A possible 'leaker'

The galaxy may also be leaking ultraviolet light. Some of the high-energy ultraviolet photons from early galaxies had to escape into space to help clear the neutral hydrogen fog of the early universe during the cosmic reionization period. Several signs suggest MARTA 3887 has porous gas through which such light could escape. About 44% of the Lyman-alpha light produced by the galaxy escapes, which is a high fraction. Because they cannot yet measure the escape fraction of the ultraviolet photons, the team calls MARTA 3887 an indirect "leaker candidate."

Overall, this black hole candidate extends the individually detected population of actively feeding black holes into the faint, metal-poor, low-mass host regime, and suggests that its growth may have outpaced the buildup of its stars.

Silver briefly forms a rare crystal structure seen in radioactive polonium

How atoms are arranged in a material shapes many of its properties. The same carbon atoms, for example, can form diamond and graphite depending on how they are arranged, giving rise to materials with vastly different chemical and physical properties. Now, researchers at Hokkaido University have discovered a new crystal structure of silver with unusually high chemical reactivity. The findings, published in Nano Letters, could open new avenues for exploring materials with desirable properties.

Silver normally forms a repeating cube-shaped structure, with atoms located at each of the cube's eight corners and at the center of each face. This arrangement is known as a face-centered cubic crystal structure and is common among metals, including aluminum, copper and gold. In the new study, researchers observed that under certain conditions, silver atoms can adopt a simple cubic structure, in which the atoms occupy only the eight corners of a cube that repeats in three dimensions.

Simple cubic structures are exceptionally rare among elements. One other example is the radioactive element polonium.

In this study, researchers used an electron beam to trigger the decomposition of silver iodide, observing the newly formed silver atoms arrange themselves into a previously unreported simple cubic structure.

At the nanoscale, where materials measure just a few billionths of a meter, structures that are unstable in larger materials can sometimes emerge temporarily. Studying these structures gives researchers an opportunity to discover materials with unique properties that are not found in their conventional forms.

Under high-vacuum conditions, the new simple cubic silver behaved differently from ordinary silver. While conventional face-centered cubic silver remained stable, simple cubic silver gradually oxidized to form silver oxide. This indicated unusually high chemical reactivity in the new structure.

"It was surprising to find that such a low-density structure could form in a pure metal crystal," says first author Dr. Masaya Sakakibara. "We expected silver nanoparticles to form when silver iodide decomposes under electron beam irradiation, but we didn't expect them to adopt a simple cubic structure."

The team used a transmission electron microscope (TEM) both to trigger the chemical transformation of silver iodide and to observe the process at the atomic scale. A TEM uses a beam of electrons with wavelengths shorter than those of visible light, allowing it to reveal individual atoms. By combining the ability to induce chemical change with real-time atomic-scale imaging, the researchers could directly observe how the new silver crystal structure emerged. "Within 100 seconds of its formation, it began to transform into silver oxide," adds Sakakibara.

"This is a new approach to discovering previously unknown crystal structures, which could also help us develop materials with novel properties in the future," says professor Yuki Kimura, co-author of the study and head of the Low Temperature Nanomaterial Science Laboratory at Hokkaido University. "Going forward, we will continue investigating the physical and chemical properties of simple cubic silver in greater detail and extend this approach to other elements and compounds."

Why it is here: original reporting, useful vocabulary

All people carry differences in their DNA that could affect how they respond to medication, according to my team’s newly published research. Moreover, 1 in 4 already take a medication their body processes differently because of their genetics.

Clinicians often take a trial and error approach to prescriptions. Two people take the same medicine at the same dose. One starts feeling better, but the other experiences side effects or sees little benefit. For some medications, part of the reason behind that difference in response is written in a person’s DNA.

The field of pharmacogenomics studies how variations in your DNA contribute to how your body processes and responds to medicines. For instance, genes can influence how quickly your liver breaks down a drug and how long it stays in your bloodstream.

But using genetic testing to guide prescriptions is not yet routine. Part of the problem is a lack of large population data to study this approach more broadly. Clinicians don’t know when it’s best to order genetic testing. And because most genetic research has been done on people of European ancestry, researchers know less about how common key gene variants are in everyone else.

Genetic Variants and Drugs

To improve the diversity of pharmacogenomic data, my team of researchers and I analyzed the whole genome sequences and health records of nearly 100,000 participants in the All of Us Research Program. All of Us is an effort from the National Institutes of Health to study the health of 1 million or more people across the U.S. and its territories, with a focus on groups historically left out of biomedical research.

We examined 16 genes with well-established links to how someone responds to different medications, pairing this data with electronic health records to identify which drugs participants had already taken.

We found that every participant carried at least one relevant genetic variant, and many carried several. Around 99.5% of participants had a genetic variant for which the Food and Drug Administration or medical guidelines recommend a different drug or change in dose for certain medications.

Even more telling, about 24% had taken a drug that is affected by a genetic variant they carried. Common examples included drugs used to reduce excess stomach acid, such as omeprazole and pantoprazole, and statins used to lower cholesterol levels. Because health records can be incomplete, our results likely underestimate the actual prevalence of these gene-drug interactions.

These findings can help improve the databases clinicians and researchers use routinely in research. We identified 17,704 previously unreported variants in the regions of these genes that encode proteins. Computer models predicted that about a quarter may have significant effects on how the body processes drugs.

Our team also reported the frequencies of hundreds of genetic variants linked to drug response for people from genetic ancestries that previously had incomplete data.

Improving Precision Medicine

Overall, our research shows that DNA variation is very common, and broader genetic testing may help optimize the medications clinicians prescribe to patients. It’s also an example of how big initiatives such as the All of Us Research Program can advance precision medicine.

However, this study doesn’t prove testing would improve outcomes for each of these people. Additionally, genes are only one factor; age, kidney and liver function, and other medications also affect how the body processes drugs.

Still, I believe the direction of the research is clear. Pharmacogenomics can provide potentially relevant benefits for many people who take medications.

item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Clean-up failed for this item, so the body is a truncated excerpt of the original.)

Why it is here: Clear reporting on a significant health study with useful vocabulary and context.

Cannabidiol not effective for treating severe behavioral problems in children with intellectual disabilities

Gaby Clark

Scientific Editor

Andrew Zinin

Chief Editor

A world-first randomized controlled trial has found that cannabidiol—commonly referred to as CBD—is not effective in treating severe behavioral problems in children with intellectual disability.

Published in JAMA Pediatrics, the Australian-led trial found that CBD was not effective in treating severe behavioral problems, such as anxiety, sleep disturbance, irritability, aggression, self-injury or elopement (wandering or running away), in children with intellectual disability aged between 6 and 18 years, as reported by parents using a standardized checklist.

It found that, in this cohort, adverse effects associated with taking CBD are mild and infrequent. Excessive drowsiness, insomnia, diarrhea and decreased appetite were the most commonly reported.

Cannabidiol is a non-intoxicating compound extracted from the cannabis or hemp plant that does not contain tetrahydrocannabinol, the compound which causes a 'high.' It has become a popular product worldwide represented by a multibillion-dollar industry. Until now, there have been few studies focused on CBD for severe behavioral problems in children with intellectual disability, and no randomized controlled trials—the gold standard for assessing whether a treatment is effective.

The study was led by Murdoch Children's Research Institute in Melbourne and included researchers from the University of Sydney and Monash University.

Elizabeth Elliott, professor of pediatrics and child health at the University of Sydney and consultant pediatrician at the Sydney Children's Hospitals Network, recruited, treated and assessed the Sydney cohort. She said, "Many children with intellectual disability experience severe behavioral problems, including irritability, aggression and self-injury. Some parents tell us they spend a significant amount on CBD in an effort to help their children, despite a lack of evidence for its effectiveness.

"CBD has recently become a popular alternative therapy, given that many medications, including antipsychotics, psychostimulants and antidepressants, are common in this group with limited impact and a risk of adverse effects.

"Many parents hoped CBD would be a solution, given its low risk of adverse effects and the perception that it is a more natural option. However, our study showed that CBD is ineffective in treating these behavioral problems in children with intellectual disability.

"Rigorous testing of alternative therapies, such as CBD, is essential, both to avoid creating false hope and to ensure resources are directed toward developing and funding access to effective treatments."

Monash University professor Katrina Williams said, "We wanted to investigate a therapy that might help the many families with a child or young person whose behavior creates risks and challenges in everyday life. We know existing interventions can be costly, time-consuming or have side effects that many people find difficult to tolerate.

"Despite early promise, cannabidiol is not an effective intervention for these families, children and young people. It is important to establish this, so families can avoid the opportunity costs and financial burden of cannabidiol treatment, and efforts can instead focus on alternative ways to support them."

While 84% of the 131 participants were diagnosed with autism, the study did not focus on any one particular genetic or developmental condition. Instead, it focused on children with intellectual disability associated with a range of diagnoses and behavioral difficulties.

In the United States, several studies have documented families using CBD to manage behavioral and psychological difficulties in children with autism and other neurodevelopmental conditions, despite limited clinical evidence. In a 2023 survey, nearly one-third of parents of children with ADHD, autism and/or anxiety had given their child unlicensed CBD products. Another study of U.S. health records suggests that about one-third of children receiving pharmaceutical CBD may be receiving it without a recorded FDA-approved indication.

How the trial worked

The study was a parallel-design, double-blind, placebo-controlled randomized clinical trial conducted over four years, between 2021 and 2025.

It involved 131 children and adolescents aged between 6 and 18 years, diagnosed with intellectual disability and severe behavioral problems. Participants were recruited from three children's hospitals: the Royal Children's Hospital in Melbourne, Monash Children's Hospital in Melbourne and The Children's Hospital at Westmead in Sydney.

Of the participants, 25.2% were female and 74.8% were male. Participants were randomly assigned to receive either CBD isolate in oil (the purest form available, dosed at 10 mg per kilogram per day) or a placebo orally for eight weeks, followed by a four-week follow-up period. Parents reported scores on the Aberrant Behavior Checklist Irritability (ABC-I) subscale, which were assessed at the end of the eight-week maintenance phase.

Earlier this year, a major University of Sydney-led study found no evidence to suggest medicinal cannabis is effective for depression, anxiety or PTSD in adults. Medicinal cannabis is an umbrella term that refers to both CBD and THC products.

Lipodystrophy is a serious metabolic disease characterized by abnormal lipid storage in the body. "Our findings thus provide new insights into the molecular mechanisms of lipid storage and cellular lipid metabolism." These latest findings can help improve understanding of the role of caveolin-1 in the development of lipodystrophy.

Intermittent fasting helps injured muscles regenerate in mice

In a new study from Koç University, alternating days of fasting and feeding helped injured muscles regenerate in mice by encouraging repair cells to multiply and fuse into muscle fibers. The effect depended on a molecular pathway previously linked to muscle wasting in cancer.

The findings suggest that the same signaling machinery can contribute to rebuilding or breaking down muscle, depending on the circumstances. Dilsad H. Arabaci, Melis Sucuoglu, Serkan Kir and colleagues at Koç University in Istanbul have published the work in Cell Reports.

Muscle repair relies on adult stem cells called satellite cells. After an injury, they produce descendants that multiply and merge to form or repair muscle fibers. The researchers investigated how cyclical changes in food availability influence this process.

More cells join the repair

The researchers changed the feeding patterns of young adult male mice by alternating 24 hours without food and 24 hours of unrestricted feeding. Control mice could eat whenever they wanted. To compare recovery from similar injuries, the team injected all mice with a muscle-damaging toxin into a lower-leg muscle.

The feeding schedule began before injury and continued during recovery. Ten days after injury, the fasting group's damaged muscles had regained more weight and contained larger regenerating fibers than those of the controls. Labeling newly dividing cells showed that more of their nuclei had become incorporated into muscle fibers.

On feeding days, these mice ate nearly twice the control group's usual daily amount, largely compensating for their fasts. Their weight dropped during fasting and recovered during feeding.

The benefit depended on an active repair process. Uninjured muscles showed no comparable increase in satellite cells or fiber size. Separate experiments also found benefits when fasting began only after injury.

A signal with two sides

Fasting increased the RNA messages used to make EDA2R, a protein that receives signals at the cell surface. Activating this receptor in cultured mouse muscle cells stimulated a signaling protein called NIK, which increased production of Myomixer—a protein that helps muscle-building cells fuse. Reducing Myomixer blocked the extra fusion.

The mouse experiments reflected this connection. Mice lacking EDA2R, or lacking NIK specifically in satellite cells and their descendants, still regenerated muscle but lost the additional benefit associated with intermittent fasting.

Yet the team's earlier research showed that the same pathway helped drive muscle wasting in tumor-bearing mice. The authors propose that brief activation in cells rebuilding muscle may have a different effect than sustained signaling in mature muscle.

"We reasoned that short fasting cycles could improve myogenic fusion, while intermittent refeeding supports this activity by providing the necessary energy and nutrients," the researchers wrote.

A separate experiment in a mouse model of Duchenne muscular dystrophy produced mixed results. Fasting increased signs of regeneration and improved grip strength relative to body weight at two of four weekly assessments. However, those mice ate less overall and grew more slowly, complicating interpretation of the benefits.

The injury experiments did not establish whether the larger regenerating fibers produced more force, and the study does not show that fasting improves muscle repair in people.

The molecular findings do suggest another treatment possibility, however: Activating the repair signals without restricting food. That would require finding a way to encourage regeneration while avoiding the muscle-wasting effects associated with prolonged activation of the same pathway.

32% of postpartum women report needing mental health care in survey spanning 16 states

Mental health conditions are the leading cause of pregnancy-related death in the United States. Yet almost all these deaths are considered preventable if women are effectively screened during and after giving birth and then connected with needed care, according to CDC data from 2017–2019.

Now, a study out in Women's Health Issues finds that the biggest barriers to mental health care for women surveyed are common economic and structural issues, such as not being able to get time off work, access affordable child care or find information about where to go for help. The study also found that asking women directly whether they need mental health care, rather than relying on screening or diagnoses, reveals that more women need care than was previously known.

"We found that the percentage of women who say they need mental health care is higher than most estimates of mood and anxiety disorders in women after giving birth, which are typically based on screening results or diagnoses," said lead author Rebecca Gourevitch, an assistant professor at the University of Maryland in the School of Public Health's Department of Health Policy and Management.

"Accessing mental health care after giving birth shouldn't be a life-and-death issue," Gourevitch said. "This study shows that in addition to current screening tools, it is also essential that women get the chance to report their own mental health needs."

The study found 32% of women self-reported a need for mental health care. Other studies using screenings and diagnoses as measures estimate 10%–20% of women have postpartum mood and anxiety disorders, with differing rates depending on the population and data source. Rates of accessing needed care were even lower among women who had Medicaid, were uninsured or were Hispanic or Asian/Pacific Islander, among other groups.

Current federal and state policy efforts focus on improving insurance access, lowering cost of services and increasing screenings to ensure access to appropriate mental health services.

"Three-quarters of women who couldn't access the mental health care they needed said they faced logistical barriers. This suggests that we should invest more in the policies that remove those barriers, such as paid family leave, paid sick leave, affordable child care and telemedicine," said Gourevitch.

The study drew on surveys from over 13,000 women from the 2022 Pregnancy Risk Assessment and Monitoring System, data that is representative of postpartum women across 16 states. The research team examined the following three self-reported questions: need for postpartum mental health care, access to needed postpartum mental health care and barriers to postpartum mental health care among those who did not access needed care.

"Focusing on women's experience of their own mental health meant this survey identified women who may not meet clinical criteria of mental health disorders, or who may not have access to services to get diagnosed, but are still in need of care," said Gourevitch.

Gourevitch warns that even the high rate of postpartum women needing care may be an undercount, as people may not self-report mental health needs for various reasons: not recognizing the symptoms, negative experiences such as discrimination within the health system or because of the stigma associated with mental health issues in general.

"The biggest logistical barrier was not having time to get care, something every new mom can relate to. When you're recovering from birth and caring for a newborn, your own care can be the first thing to go. This study helps pinpoint the barriers we can address to make mental health support fit into new moms' lives," said senior author Marie E. Thoma, an associate professor in the SPH Department of Family Science.

Thoma also leads the Women's Health Interdisciplinary Research Collaborative (WHIRC), a 2026 UMD Grand Challenges institutional awardee.

A man with paranoid schizophrenia who killed three people while experiencing a psychotic episode had been released from custody after a “catalogue of failures” by police and medical professionals, an investigation has found.

Alexander Lewis-Ranwell was arrested and released twice by police in the 48 hours before he killed Anthony Payne, 80, and the twin brothers Roger and Dick Carter, 84, in their homes in Exeter in 2019.

Officers were found to have ignored warnings from a national database as well as a mental health assessor, according to a joint investigation by the Sunday Times and BBC Radio 4’s File On 4 Investigates.

Numerous failings were found in hours of police video, detention logs and witness testimony. The medical professional who was sent to examine Lewis-Ranwell, 27, did not have expertise in mental health and dismissed his unpredictable behaviour.

There were also failures to record and share key details that would have built up a picture of the severity of Lewis-Ranwell’s mental illness.

Officers did not know that by law they had the power to detain him under the Mental Health Act without a medical assessment. Warnings from Lewis-Ranwell’s mother, that he was having a psychotic episode and should be kept in custody, were also ignored.

The families of the three men have called on the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) to open an investigation into Devon and Cornwall police, but they are still waiting for answers and an apology.

The watchdog has said that the force should investigate itself, but they have heard nothing for two years.

Two days before the murders took place, Lewis-Ranwell was arrested after breaking into a farm. After his release he was arrested a second time for attacking a farmer with a 1.2-metre (4ft) logging saw.

Despite exhibiting disturbing behaviour in custody – police bodycam footage shows him semi-naked, hissing, spitting and punching at the hatch window to his cell, while ranting about paedophiles and seeing animals – he was released again.

Following a rampage that lasted hours and in which he threatened multiple people, he killed the three men, bludgeoning Payne with a hammer and killing the twins with a spade.

A trial at Exeter crown court in December 2019 found Lewis-Ranwell not guilty by reason of insanity. He was given a hospital restriction order, where he will stay until agencies are confident he could be released back into the community.

One psychiatrist who studied the case told the court he believed Lewis-Ranwell, a former public schoolboy from Croyde, north Devon, was “one of the illest people” he had come across.

Last month an inquest found failings by police led to his release after a doctor missed “clear signs of delusion and disordered thinking”.

Amanda Taylor told the Sunday Times that her family was still seeking justice for her uncles the Carter brothers and that they want the IOPC to revisit the case.

“All I want is for just one of the agencies involved to stand up and say: ‘We are so sorry. Serious mistakes were made. We recognise the devastating consequences of those failures and we will do everything in our power to make sure this never happens again,’” she said.

Lewis-Ranwell’s case is one of several where failures from the police and mental health services to manage risk have resulted in tragedy.

A review by the Care Quality Commission of the treatment of Valdo Calocane, who has paranoid schizophrenia and killed three people in Nottingham in 2023, concluded that a “series of errors and misjudgments” led to him being discharged, despite repeatedly not taking medication and showing signs of aggression.

The report concluded that there are “systemic issues with community mental health care which, without immediate action, will continue to pose an inherent risk to patient and public safety”.

NHS England has since strengthened guidance around community mental health support for people with severe mental illnesses who face high risk or struggle to engage with services.

Noting that there are an estimated 100 to 120 mental health-related killings in the UK every year, Julian Hendy, of the victims’ charity Hundred Families, said: “In my view, had the lessons in the Lewis-Ranwell case been learnt earlier, and effective action taken, there is a real chance that the Nottingham attacks could well have been prevented. Services aren’t learning and totally innocent people are losing their lives as a result.”

A police spokesperson said the force was addressing “areas of learning” and would reflect on the recommendations of the inquest jury, adding: “Our thoughts, as always, remain with the loved ones of Anthony Payne and Dick and Roger Carter.”

GL.iNet Security Notice 2026-11-20

SECURITY NOTICE · CUSTOMER ADVISORY

GL.iNet Router and KVM Security Incident

Issued | Last updated

On November 20, 2026, GL.iNet identified a vulnerability in its cloud remote management services. An unauthorized party exploited the vulnerability to access and install malicious software on some GL.iNet routers and KVM devices.

The attack path has been blocked. We fixed the cloud vulnerability and blocked the access used in this incident. Devices can no longer be newly infected through this attack path. These measures do not remove malware from devices that were already infected.

What you should do

Security firmware: Stable firmware with security fixes for both routers and KVM devices is scheduled for . We recommend installing the stable update for your model as soon as it becomes available, even if the check finds no signs of infection.

Follow the steps below to check your device. For both routers and KVM devices, look for the exact text crond -i /tmp/.log within the details of a running process. The process entry may contain other information.

- If you find the indicator: Treat your device as infected. For a KVM, you can install the security beta for your model now using the links below. You can also restore your device to factory settings to address the infection. A factory reset erases your settings and requires you to set up the device again. The cloud vulnerability has been fixed, so a reset device cannot be reinfected through that vulnerability. Whether you install the beta or reset your device, we still recommend installing the latest stable security firmware for your model as soon as it is available.

- If the check completes without finding the indicator: If you have no other reason to suspect infection, no factory reset or other cleanup is needed. The stable security update is still recommended.

- If you cannot complete the check or are unsure about the result: Contact support@gl-inet.com for help.

How to check a GL.iNet router

Option 1: Use the web admin panel (LuCI)

- In the router’s Admin Panel, go to System → Advanced Settings and sign in to LuCI.

- In LuCI, open Status → Processes.

- Press Ctrl+F (Command+F on macOS) and search for tmp/.log. Check whether a matching process shows crond -i /tmp/.log.

Option 2: Use SSH

Sign in to your router via SSH and run:

ps | grep tmp

Look for crond -i /tmp/.log in the output. A line showing only the grep command is not a match.

How to check a GL.iNet KVM

In the KVM web interface, go to Toolbox → Terminal → Access. Run the command for your model in the KVM’s terminal, not on the connected computer.

RMQ1:

ps -a | grep tmp

All other KVM models:

ps -aux | grep tmp

Look for crond -i /tmp/.log in the output. A line showing only the grep command is not a match.

If your KVM is infected, also check the connected computer

As a precaution, check for unfamiliar programs, browser extensions or user accounts; unexpected startup items or scheduled tasks; and unusual settings changes or network activity. Run a full scan with up-to-date security software.

KVM security firmware downloads

KVM security fixes are already available through the beta channel for the models listed below. If your KVM shows signs of infection, you can install the beta update for your model now.

item.title: QCon San Francisco 2026: The Harness Is the New Operating System
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Technical discussion on AI agent development

At QCon San Francisco 2026, Manju Rajashekhar, founder and CEO of Mad Labs, opened the conference with the keynote "The Harness Is the New Operating System."

Rajashekhar argued that the harness around an AI model, rather than the model itself, decides what an agent can do and how safely it does it. Each part of a harness, the keynote proposed, maps onto a job that operating systems already perform.

Rajashekhar began with a split that shaped computing history. Applications encoded behavior, while operating systems abstracted the hardware beneath them, and that separation made portable, composable software possible.

AI agents break that arrangement because they generate behavior at runtime. Software therefore needs a new layer that makes that behavior useful, reliable and repeatable, and Rajashekhar called that layer the harness.

In Rajashekhar's framing, model plus harness equals agent, and the harness is "everything in an agent that isn't the model." It supplies the tasks, context, tools, state, permissions, feedback loops and a definition of done.

The model supplies capability. The harness turns that capability into dependable software.

The simplest agent is a model running in a loop that the harness controls. But "a loop isn't enough. Every iteration has to count," and Rajashekhar described four parts of the loop that make each iteration count.

Context works like virtual memory. The harness assembles what the model needs for its next decision inside the hard limit of the context window, and the advice was to "give the model a pointer, not the whole thing."

The interface works like system calls and "puts a ceiling on the agent's effective capability." Rajashekhar pointed to the SWE-agent paper, in which GPT-4 Turbo resolved 11.0% of SWE-bench Lite issues through a plain shell and 18.0% through an interface designed for agents.

Execution works like processes and permissions. The harness enforces boundaries through isolation and scoped credentials, such as a test database with no production access, because "instructions guide. Boundaries enforce."

Feedback works like return codes. The harness keeps "tests failed," "could not run" and "outcome unknown" apart, so the model does not have to guess what happened.

That matters because errors compound. On a 20-step task with a 95% chance of each step going right, the whole job succeeds 36% of the time, and catching 80% of errors lifts that to 82%.

When an agent goes in circles, Rajashekhar said, most engineers swap the model. A better first step is to keep the model and change the harness.

DeepSeek's model card for DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash reports the same model scoring from 65.5% to 74.2% on DeepSWE across eight harnesses. The minimal harnesses scored highest, which Rajashekhar read as a sign that more harness is not automatically better.

In a second study, Qwen3.8-27B passed 66.8% of 100 hard LiveCodeBench problems with a single call. Inside a manager-worker scaffold with a shared ledger, it passed 92.4%.

Rajashekhar made a related point on LinkedIn earlier this year. Frontier models are forgiving, the post said, while "open-weight models are less forgiving. They make you think deeply about the harness and how it aligns to the model."

The harness also determines what an agent is allowed to affect. Rajashekhar contrasted an agent that fixes failing tests with one that deletes the tests so they pass, observing that "the difference isn't ability. It's authority."

The example offered was the July 2026 incident in which OpenAI evaluation agents on a capture-the-flag benchmark reached the internet through an open code sandbox. They held admin access on Hugging Face's internal clusters for about two and a half days.

Human approval alone is a weak gate, Rajashekhar argued, citing Anthropic's work on Claude Code auto mode, which InfoQ covered in May. People approve the large majority of permission prompts, and "a tired gatekeeper is a rubber stamp."

The keynote extended a talk Rajashekhar gave at QCon AI Boston 2026. That talk argued that production agents "are just distributed systems in disguise" and proposed the actor model as their runtime.

In the Boston design, each agent task owns its state, receives events through a mailbox, writes each state change to a durable store and runs under a supervisor. The talk closed with a variation on Greenspun's tenth rule, suggesting that any sufficiently complicated agent loop contains half of an actor system.

The San Francisco keynote widened the lens from the runtime to everything the model sees, calls and runs inside. Rajashekhar brings a systems background to that question, having led caching systems on Twitter's early engineering team, which open-sourced twemproxy.

The talk arrives as "harness" has become the common term for everything around the model. Thoughtworks Distinguished Engineer Birgitta Böckeler described it in a February memo as covering "the tooling and practices we can use to keep AI agents in check."

Rajashekhar closed on why a harness design is never finished. Every component "encodes an assumption about what the model can't do," and those assumptions expire as models improve.

Anthropic's harness for long-running apps needed context resets because Claude Sonnet 4.5 showed "context anxiety" near its context limit. That behavior largely disappeared with Opus 4.5, as InfoQ reported in April.

The reverse also holds. LangChain moved checks the model kept skipping into the harness and lifted GPT-5.2-Codex from 52.8% to 66.5% on Terminal-Bench 2.0 without changing the model.

The responsibility stays. The mechanism changes.

Rajashekhar asked attendees to open an agent they already use and read its system prompt and tool list. Then, on a task where it struggles, change one part of the loop and rerun what already worked.

Developers interested in learning more can watch InfoQ in the coming weeks for video of the keynote and can view the keynote abstract and resources here.

item.title: Can you safely use a 140w charger on an iPhone?
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Explanation of iPhone charger compatibility

Can you safely use a 140w charger on an iPhone?

The simple answer is yes, an iPhone can tolerate a 140-watt charger, but it's not a simple process, and there are safety considerations. A 140-watt charger is an upper limit that your iPhone will never reach because even the latest iPhone 18 Pro hits its cap at 52W. An iPhone can only pull what it can pull, and it's nowhere near 140W. USB PD used to top out at 100W, but the newer range is between 100W and 240W, now known as Extended Power Range (EPR). EPR adds 28V, 36V and 48V options. Once a device is in EPR mode, it has to send a "keep-alive" message every half second. If the charger doesn't receive that message, it drops back down to 5V. An iPhone's requirements are well below that threshold.

Potential safety issues are generally on the charger's end. Apple is pretty blunt about using third-party chargers that fail to meet safety standards, claiming it could cause injury and even death. Obviously, that's something iPhone users should avoid, so stick with reputable brands. Yes, Apple's own power adapters and cables are priced like they have 24k gold in them, but there are plenty of options out there that meet safety standards and cost much less.

So how many watts does your iPhone want?

Far less than 140W. The iPhone 17, 17 Pro and 17 Pro Max reach 50 percent in about 20 minutes with a 40W or higher adapter. The iPhone Air and iPhone 17e only need 20W to hit 50 percent in roughly half an hour. For an iPhone 15 or 16 (or an older Lightning model like the iPhone 14 with a USB-C to Lightning cable), a USB PD adapter 18W or greater is needed for fast charging. The iPhone 18 Pro series and the iPhone Duo step things up a bit. The best and fastest charger for these phones is a 60W adapter with Adjustable Voltage Supply (AVS) and USB PD 3.2, plus a USB-C cable that can handle 60W or more.

None of that approaches 140W. The best use case for 140W+ is a high-performance laptop or charging several devices at the same time. If you have an Apple adapter (Apple doesn't supply them with iPhones/iPads for environmental purposes), the wattage is printed on the top or bottom. Apple prints the Dynamic Power Symbol on their 40W chargers. You can also get a fairly accurate estimate of charging time directly from your iPhone. On iOS 18 or later, a Slow Charger message appears on the Lock Screen and under Settings > Battery. iOS 26 ramps up the convenience by alerting you when you're using an incompatible charger that isn't charging your iPhone.

How many watts is a typical USB port?

Not much, unless it's a USB-C port with Power Delivery. At base specs, USB 2.0 ports supply 5V at 500mA or 2.5W. USB 3.0 and 3.1 ports bump it up to 900mA or 4.5W. The Battery Charging 1.2 spec ports can reach 1.5A or 7.5W. If you prefer to charge from a PC or laptop, it's a bit chaotic. For instance, orange ports on Intel NUC PCs are rated at 1.5A, and the blue ones are 900 milliamps. Black ports are typically USB 2.0 and have a modest 2.5W default. Those examples sound pretty sluggish because they are. Plug an iPhone 18 Pro Max into a USB 2.0, and it's gonna be a while. The iPhone 15 and later are capped at 7.5W on a USB-A charger. Fortunately, USB-C is a major upgrade over USB-A, with 15W (5V at 3A) without Power Delivery.

With Power Delivery, it skyrockets to 100W in the Standard Power Range and 240W with EPR. On top of that, standard USB-C cables are rated for 3A, hitting their ceiling at 60W, while 100W feature e-marked 5A cables. These cables have a tiny chip that tells the charger what it can handle. EPR cables encompass everything above 100W. A "typical USB port" is ultimately defined by the individual. For someone who uses a fairly standard 20W adapter for an iPhone, a USB-A port may be considered typical, but a specialized USB-A charger can push up to 18W. In other words, what is "typical" depends on what you're using and what you're used to.

This free app connects your Android phone to your Windows PC wirelessly

No subscriptions, accounts or extra programs taking up space on your PC.

Moving files between an Android phone and a Windows PC is broadly a solved problem. You can use a cloud service like Google Drive as an intermediary, although uploading from one device and downloading on the other can be time-consuming. Connecting via USB is also an option, though you lose the convenience of a wireless connection. Quick Share on Android offers a good middle ground, letting you transfer files directly.

None of these help if you need to do more than move files around, though. For that, you'll need third-party programs that offer more features, like a media browser and phone mirroring. The downside is that they often require installing software on both devices and often charge a subscription fee. PlainApp, though, is different: it's a free, open-source program that lets you view and manage your Android phone's files on your computer — without installing any additional software on your PC. It also doesn't ask you to create an account or log in.

PlainApp is available on the Play Store and supports phones running Android 9 or newer. To use it, install the app, grant it notification and file access permissions and note the URL it displays. As long as your computer is connected to the same Wi-Fi network as your Android phone, you can access your phone's files wirelessly through any web browser at that URL.

Everything you can do with PlainApp

PlainApp uses a self-signed TLS certificate, so your browser will show a warning the first time you access the URL. Click on Advanced > Proceed to bypass this warning. Finally, click Log in and tap Allow on your phone when prompted. Once connected, you can view and manage images, videos, music and contacts stored on your Android phone straight from your computer's browser.

The web app's user interface is simple but modern enough to feel like a polished application rather than a basic file transfer utility. The Files tab lets you browse all accessible folders and files, as well as transfer files both ways. You can send text to your phone's clipboard, call a number directly from the web GUI and use a screen-mirroring feature that shows your phone's screen in your computer's browser. PlainApp says that remote control is possible here — much like iPhone Mirroring on macOS — but I couldn't get it to work on my phone.

PlainApp's media viewer handles images and videos and shows them in original quality. If your browser does not support HEVC video playback, PlainApp will automatically convert the video to H.264. You can also use the built-in image editor, which offers basic tools for cropping, adding text or drawing directly on your photos. There's also a music player if audio's more your thing. Overall, while Quick Share is still faster for transferring photos or videos, PlainApp is much more versatile if you want to browse and organize more of your phone's contents wirelessly.

Why it is here: Clear reporting on a significant economic issue with useful vocabulary and context

The cold reality of cutting local tax revenue by billions of dollars a year is starting to dawn on Floridians, who voted to slash property taxes earlier this month.

Amendment 3 expands the so-called homestead exemption, shielding more of a home’s assessed value from taxation. It will nearly triple from $51,400 currently to $150,000 in 2027 and increase again to $250,000 in 2028.

It also lowers the cap on annual assessments on rental and commercial properties from a 10% hike to 5%. The amendment doesn’t apply to school-related property taxes but creates a path for abolishing non-school property taxes completely.

State economists have projected that local governments will lose nearly $5 billion in the first year and nearly $12 billion a year once the exemption is fully phased in.

To be sure, local governments can raise revenue in other ways, such sales taxes and fees. Big cities can also rely more on taxes aimed at tourists, but smaller communities will be hit especially hard with some losing the bulk of their tax base.

Cities are now scrambling to figure out how to fund vital services like police, fire fighters and paramedics as well as roads and other infrastructure with much smaller budgets.

In Deltona, City Manager Doc Dougherty told residents that the Christmas parade was canceled and blamed Amendment 3, warning that cuts wouldn’t end there. He estimated the city’s budget must be cut by $12 million in the coming year and then another $5 million the following year. By 2030, Deltona is expected to cut more than $23 million.

“Even though we have been doing everything right by reducing our tax millage for the past four years, including roll back this year, this is only the beginning of the vast reduction in City

services our residents will face for years to come,” Dougherty wrote in a letter to residents on Saturday.

He added that all city events are effectively cancelled, except for two upcoming 5K runs that are self-supporting. Deltona is also withdrawing vehicle orders, terminating construction contracts, and cancelling professional services to “meet the goal of what was voted for by the residents.”

Elsewhere in Florida, Delray Beach stopped funding its St. Patrick’s Day Parade, St. Petersburg is ending its beach trolley service, and Brevard County is targeting park maintenance, mosquito control, athletic fields, youth sports programs and playground repairs as areas for potential cuts.

Manatee County Commissioner George Kruse gave a similarly bleak assessment of the new revenue landscape. In a Substack post on Nov. 13, he estimated there will be $63 million less in tax revenue next year and $113 million less the following year.

While the state has endured past recessions and real estate crashes that shrank local tax revenue, Kruse pointed out that Amendment 3 is entirely different.

“This isn’t a cycle, this is a permanent, structural shift in how government functions. Forever,” he wrote. “A facility that closes, will stay closed. An employee going part time, will never come back full time. A ‘delay’ in a capital project used to mean later, now it means never.”

To close the massive revenue shortfall, Kruse said a “small fraction” could be covered by adjustments to fees, but the county sheriff must offer a material budget cut too.

He vowed to reject any new sales taxes or higher property tax rates that put a heavier burden on renters and small businesses, while acknowledging that reductions in services will disproportionately affect those most in need of affordability.

“But last week, 65% of Manatee voters said they wanted to forego services and quality of life for lower property taxes,” Kruse added. “So that’s how this Board needs to cover this permanent gap.”

He then went through a list of areas the county must scrutinize, including publicly owned assets, department consolidations, privatization, new infrastructure projects, special tax zones, interlocal agreement, funding for nonprofits, and even “niceties” that provide community spirit.

“That includes sponsorships, parades, movies in the park, holiday events,” Kruse explained. “Everything adds up when trying to fill such a large hole in the budget. We can’t layoff a needed employee while redirecting their salary to firework displays.”

Amendment 3 may also require the county to rethink how it develops, such as favoring rental properties in denser areas over new homes in urban sprawl that entail added infrastructure costs, he noted. But throttling housing supply will raise home prices and rents, worsening the affordability issues that Amendment 3 is supposed to address.

Outgoing Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis, who backed Amendment 3, has dismissed such warnings as “fearmongering” and suggested state grants could offset any budget shortfalls to local agencies. Many details are lacking, and DeSantis has called for a special session of the legislature to spell out exactly how the amendment will work.

But leaders in the state house have said a special session isn’t necessary, with Senate Majority Leader-designate Nick DiCeglie warning local governments against fee hikes. That means DeSantis’ successor, Governor-elect Byron Donalds, will be responsible for dealing with the fallout.

Despite the budget crunch local governments face, DeSantis also urged state lawmakers to block new taxes and fees.

“There won’t be fee hikes if the Legislature stops it. Pass a taxpayer bill of rights, limit local spending and protect against new local taxes and fees,” he posted on X on Wednesday.

That got Trump’s attention. And on Saturday, he reposted on his Truth Social account El-Sayed’s initial Nov. 12 appeal. El-Sayed posted “Let’s get to work, then.”

The gambit echoes a famous line from President Ronald Reagan in February 1988, when he spoke at a meeting of the White House Conference for a Drug Free America:

“On my desk in the Oval Office, I have a little sign that says: There is no limit to what a man can do or where he can go if he doesn’t mind who gets the credit.”

While similar statements have been attributed to others going back more than 100 years, Reagan’s line is notable as it came during the modern era of American politics, which has grown even more intensely partisan since then.

In fact, during the midterm election campaign, Trump ramped up the partisan rancor to such a level that he called El-Sayed a “jihadist” who was “on the side of the terrorists.”

But the incoming Democratic senator is ready to set that aside for the sake of expanding health coverage. On Sunday, El-Sayed noted Trump “signaled openness to the opportunity,” telling NBC’s Meet the Press with Kristen Welker that while growing up playing lacrosse, he was taught to play the ball, not the man.

El-Sayed also predicted that if Trump says he wants TrumpCare for all and is open to signing legislation, then a lot of Republicans in Congress will vote for it.

When asked later if he has any plans to meet with Trump or Vice President JD Vance, El-Sayed replied “those plans are in the works.”

Minnesota Senator-Elect Peggy Flanagan, another Democrat who rode the blue tsunami, voiced similar willingness to capitalize on Trump’s desire to name things after himself.

Why it is here: Unique and interesting topic with vivid descriptions and cultural context

My great-great-grandfather came to the Tuscan ghost island of Pianosa as a prisoner.

The island lives up to its name, I thought as my ferry drifted toward the sole dock on this protected isola fantasma. “Pianosa” is derived from piano, Italian for “flat,” and indeed the island crouches low to the cyan Tyrrhenian Sea, its shores fringed by parasol pines and deserted prison watchtowers. From 1856 to 1998, Pianosa was a remote penal colony—and the place where my ancestor, Salvatore Giovanni Pellegrino Irace, died.

I’d learned this family lore thanks to a partnership between Ancestry, the Blackstone-owned leader in the at-home DNA-testing space, and Kensington, a bespoke travel outfitter, which invited me to test-drive its Personal Heritage Journey. After I submitted a DNA sample, Ancestry got to work filling in my Italian family tree, with researchers combing archives in Tuscany, Molise, and Campania. “So the interesting thing about Salvatore,” genealogist Kyle Betit said on our initial call, “is that he died in prison of tuberculosis in 1894—and we don’t know why he was there.”

Who doesn’t love a good family mystery? That’s part of what draws clients to Kensington’s genealogical-based trips. The journeys average $20,000 to $25,000 per person, with the company’s travel desk handling all the details in high style.

For me, that meant a chartered boat from mainland Tuscany to the island of Elba; chauffeured SUVs between regions; a private guide in Pompeii; and some spectacular accommodations, including Casa Angelina and Palazzo Avino on the Amalfi Coast. The major flex, though, was having a professional genealogist, Gabriele Musumeci, riding shotgun.

Once upon a time, possessing one’s comprehensive genealogy was a signal of wealth and pedigree. Then, in the 2000s, the rise of at-home DNA-testing kits from Ancestry and 23andMe made such knowledge commonplace. The ultrawealthy can now seek out deeper stories through first-person ancestry tourism, from China to Ghana. Kensington reports that demand has doubled and revenue has quadrupled in five years. Grand View Research put the global value of “heritage tourism”—of which ancestral travel is a segment—at $625 billion in 2025. It’s expected to reach almost a trillion by 2033.

“I think there’s a deep need in any of us to understand who we are,” Musumeci said as we descended the concrete steps to Pianosa’s white-sand beach, Cala Giovanna. “For most Americans, your story is cut.” He made a chopping motion. And then a sewing motion: “We stitch it back together.”

Most luxury travel planners now offer some variety of ancestry service. Alexandrea Padilha, director at the membership-based Fischer Unlimited, recently hired genealogists in Germany and the U.S. to trace a Louisiana tech entrepreneur’s ancestry. The results were bound into a book for the client’s father’s 80th birthday and also informed the itinerary for a trip to Germany—a way to show younger family members their roots. “I think that’s grounding for young adults today,” Padilha says, “living in a world that’s slowly slipping away.”

Existential dread is one hell of a motivator. “When it feels like the world may be shifting every second, people reach for something enduring,” says Dr. Katie Blake, a Texas-based social psychologist who specializes in travel. “The archives give you the facts, but it’s the place itself that gives you the identity pull that’s different than something you just see on paper.”

A sudden, biblical rainstorm broke open during our mile-long bike ride from Cala Giovanna to Pianosa’s imposing Agrippa Prison. We sheltered inside the Zante wing, where prisoners like Salvatore slept four to a concrete cell on metal beds, as thunder rattled the rusty gates.

My itinerary traced Salvatore’s life backward. A few days later, Musumeci and I rendezvoused in Molise, where Salvatore grew up. My great-great-great-grandfather, Vincenzo, moved his family to Montenero di Bisaccia, a mountain keep surrounded by vineyards and wheat fields sloping down to the Adriatic, in 1838, when Salvatore was a boy. At Montenero’s city hall, the clerks hauled out massive, crimson-bound books, and Musumeci leafed through until he found the birth and marriage records of Salvatore’s second son, Giuseppe—my great-grandfather.

Walking through Montenero’s hilltop puzzle of alleys brought those pieces of paper to life—and conjured a story of downward mobility. Along the town’s outer promenade, ringing the remains of medieval stone walls, a lookout faced the amber foothills where Vincenzo bought land and a farmhouse. I walked the narrow alley the family lived on after they lost the farm. Within four years, Vincenzo had spiraled from merchant and farm owner to street sweeper. He died in 1842, leaving his son on the poverty-to-prison pipeline.

I also saw the house in the old ghetto where my great-grandmother, Nicoletta, grew up. She and Giuseppe had a daughter out of wedlock, Mattia. (Nobody in my family had known Mattia existed until Musumeci discovered her.) The infant likely died during the couple’s 1900 journey to America, where, at Ellis Island, Irace became Erace. Giuseppe and Nicoletta settled in Philadelphia and had 16—yes, 16—more children, including my paternal grandfather, Michael Erace, who died in 2013.

It was like I was looking at Grandpop Mike’s long-lost brother when we met Bruno Irace, a 74-year-old Ironman triathlete and my fourth cousin, that afternoon. Smile, hair, complexion, bone structure; it was uncanny. We sipped espresso and compared photos, then visited a cemetery where “Irace” seemed to be engraved on every other gravestone. Two Iraces were listed on an obelisk in the village park honoring fallen soldiers. When it was time to leave Montenero, Bruno told us to come back soon. “You have family here,” he said.…
