In May 2025, two of the most talked-about names in beauty joined forces. The headline-making deal brought together e.l.f. Beauty, the company that began by selling $1 makeup online more than two decades ago and turned drugstore makeup into a viral phenomenon, and rhode, a minimalist skincare line launched by Hailey Bieber—an influencer with tens of millions of followers.

Over the years, e.l.f. has grown into a $1.3 billion business (FY25) with more than two dozen consecutive quarters of market-share gains and net sales growth, expanding at a rate roughly four times that of the global beauty market. More recently, rhode became a nine-figure brand in just three years and with only ten products before being acquired by e.l.f. and making its retail debut at Sephora in September. Though established players like L’Oréal, Estée Lauder, and Coty remain far larger, with even single-digit growth translating into meaningful progress at their size, what has set e.l.f. and rhode apart is their ability to connect with Gen Z and other young consumers in ways incumbents have struggled to replicate.

Both brands have leaned into cultural and digital fluency. e.l.f. has used social media to fuel its rise, marketing affordable alternatives to premium products that regularly go viral in “get-ready-with-me" and makeup-haul review videos. rhode, meanwhile, has tapped into its founder’s celebrity profile—and related marketing power—to promote a minimalist aesthetic and a tightly edited range of products. Together, these companies are betting that the ability to move quickly with their communities is a smart path to relevance and to growth in today’s rapidly changing consumer economy.

CEOs Tarang Amin and Nick Vlahos recently spoke with strategy+business about what it takes to stay close to your customer while scaling fast, how they’re using AI for sharper insights, and why keeping an entrepreneurial spirit alive may be their most important advantage.

The following is an edited version of the conversation.

S+B: When e.l.f. and rhode came together, what did that moment mean for you?

Tarang Amin: We’d been watching rhode for some time, and the way the brand resonated with consumers was unlike anything I’d seen. When we finally sat down together, the philosophies, the culture, the focus on community—it all just clicked. That alignment made it a no-brainer.

Nick Vlahos: Tarang and I had worked together more than 20 years ago, so there was already a foundation. But the turning point was when we sat down with Hailey. We weren’t just talking business; we were talking about where our heads and hearts were, and what we wanted to build. From the beginning, it was clear that e.l.f. valued the same things we do: respect for founders, creativity, community. That gave us the confidence this was the right match.

S+B: In practical terms, how do you plan to create new value?

Amin: We’re building a portfolio of complementary yet distinct brands that all share one thing in common: they’re fast-growing and have tremendous white space ahead. Both e.l.f. and rhode are coming from positions of strength. At e.l.f., our gross margins are over 70%. rhode is already accretive to the company. So it’s not just top-line growth—it’s disciplined growth on both the top and bottom lines.

Vlahos: From our side, the most important thing is accessibility. We’re a three-year-old brand, and up until now we’ve been direct-to-consumer only. But in September, we launched in Sephora across US and Canadian stores. Over time, that’s going to be a huge unlock. And when you look at e.l.f.’s capabilities—retail relationships, global footprint, executional excellence—those are areas that can help us accelerate what we’re already doing digitally.

S+B: You’ve grown fast. How do you plan to keep up that momentum?

Vlahos: It’s definitely a challenge, and I think overcoming it starts with humility and curiosity. We focus on listening, learning, and then acting on what we hear. We’re also fortunate to work with founders like Hailey who are actively shaping the creative vision, and we’re pushing to keep evolving instead of repeating ourselves.

Amin: I’d add that even with our success, we see both challenges and opportunities ahead. Every acquisition has to be more than a financial fit. It has to match our culture and keep us agile. The key is never getting too comfortable and always adapting as fast as our consumers do.

S+B: How do you stay up to date with consumers’ evolving behavior?

Vlahos: It comes down to turning consumer signals into action. To share one example, we noticed people mixing our blush with our barrier restore cream—blending hydration with color in a way that worked for them. So we leaned into the insight and developed a hybrid blush that delivers both skin benefits and pigment. Because we’ve invested in our own labs and innovation teams—including four chemists and a packaging engineering team in Santa Monica—we’re able to go from signal to shelf at speed. We watch. We listen. Then we build. That’s how a consumer hack becomes a product, and how we keep delighting our community with what’s next.…

A survey of about 1,000 Americans found that one in 10 would describe their partner as a financial bully.

When we put out a call to out readers last week to see if any of them had similar experiences, we found that many of you wouldn’t define the actions described as financial bullying. Instead, quite a number of you insisted that keeping track of your partner’s expenses was simply budgeting and being financially responsible.

It’s not bullying, it’s vigilance

Adam: “Having disagreements about spending in a relationship is hardly bullying, it is natural and unavoidable and has happened since the dawn of money.”

Rebecca: “I thought it was called teaching financial responsibility.”

Sean: “Families should work together to maintain a budget, often one spouse is more reckless than the other, that’s not bullying, that’s being responsible.”

Sarah: “Financial bullying?! Sharing a life together and a bank account means both parties get to be involved in spending decisions.”

Nicole: “My husband knows how much money I spend. From a certain amount, I always ask him, if he’s OK with it. I won’t call it ‘financial bullying’, I call it ‘living together’. Someone has to keep an eye on the family’s money.”

There’s bullying and then there’s being passive-aggressive

Simone:

My ex-husband routinely spent our rent/bill/food money on restaurants, taxis and other things we really didn’t have the budget for. Finally I got sick of being behind on rent and always running out of money for food, and put my foot down. He refused to sit down and do a budget with me, saying “Why don’t you just do it?” So I did.

I made a budget of all his personal spending, and finally I had to make him choose between taxis to work and lunch at restaurants, which felt bizarre and incredibly uncomfortable for me. He chose taxis over lunch, and after that, whenever colleagues would ask him why he wasn’t joining them for lunch, he’d tell them that his wife wouldn’t allow it.

So my question is, who was the financial bully in this situation, me or him?

Remember: a partner’s spending habits can affect our lives for years to come

A reader from Arkansas says she was financially bullied by her then-husband for years:

But not the way you mean: when I suggested he cut back on his credit-card use on the card held in my name, he sharply increased his use, increasing our debt to $23,000 in a matter of months. That’s what I call financial bullying.

Even checking the accounts doesn’t stop financial ruin:

A few years after we were married, my ex-husband developed a drug abuse problem. I was balancing the checkbook every month. He would take money out of our accounts to buy and sell drugs and not tell me. When the accounts wouldn’t match up, he would berate me for not being accurate. He spent all of our money and ran the credit cards up to the max.

When we got divorced we had two credit cards, one for the home and one for his “business” that never got off the ground. The agreement was that I would pay off the family card and he would pay off the business card. Of course, he never did and the creditors came after me – I wound up paying both of them off. My credit was wrecked for seven years.

Some agreed that bullying does occur when the funds are not shared and enjoyed equally:

Chris:

Reading the comments here I guess none of the commentators has experienced this.

I have and it certainly was bullying. Talking about finances together is very different from keeping a tight eye on your partner’s spending and questioning every last penny. In my situation, this was coupled with a wholly one-sided approach to discussing joint spending which characterised what I suggested as ‘spending on me’ while what they wanted as ‘spending on us’.

Unless you’ve been in that sort of relationship, I recommend that you aren’t so quick to judge.

Robal agreed:

Been there too. Money I earned was “our money”, money she earned was “her money”. She was serious. She would get hysterical whenever I bought a magazine yet she felt she could blow hundreds in one shopping spree on whatever she felt like having.

The line between financially bullying and abuse can be easily crossed:

A female reader living in New York wrote:

I am in an arranged marriage, to a man who is self-made after a struggled childhood, with disregarded needs, as defined above. However, unless purchases are made to his own liking, he is extremely tight with money. For many years into my marriage – around five – I had no say in the type of food I ate or clothes I wore. My request for a choice of three types of breakfast cereals was seen as “an attempt to cremate his money”. My clothes came from Walmart or Value City.

When we went out, I was expected to eat at home, and could not have a $1 coffee or $1 hot dog in case I got a little peckish under the guise of ‘saving money’ and ‘aggressive savings targets’. If an eggplant spoiled in the refrigerator, the spoiled part was taken and smeared across my face and down my arms, to teach me the value of money. item.title: A ‘mismatch in timing’: Data center power demand is growing 19% a year. The grid is growing 2%
item.description:

Why it is here: Technical analysis of data center power demand and grid capacity

The tech industry is famous for moving fast. That collision now sits at the center of the AI buildout, a project estimated to cost trillions: Citigroup projects Big Tech will spend more than $2.8 trillion on AI infrastructure through 2029, and a Brookings study puts U.S. investment at $10.3 trillion between 2025 and 2032.

The grid isn’t built for that pace. Since 2000, power to data centers has risen an average of 19% a year while U.S. grid capacity has expanded just 2% annually, according to an analysis by insurance broker Howden. Data center power use is growing 10 times faster than the system meant to supply it.

That gap has become one of the biggest bottlenecks facing the AI industry. And after this month’s midterms, in which voters rejected data center projects almost everywhere they appeared on the ballot, power is now a political problem, too.

The grid is years behind demand

Data centers took about 5% of U.S. grid capacity in 2025. Howden estimates that to hold that share through 2030 at current growth rates, they would have to source up to 58% of their power off the grid, roughly 110 gigawatts, a level the firm itself considers unlikely.

Consumption tells the same story. Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory projects data centers could use as much as 12% of U.S. electricity by 2028, about six times their 1.9% share in 2018, before the AI boom.

Rob Gramlich, president of consulting firm Grid Strategies, told Fortune in September that there’s a real “mismatch in timing” between how quickly data centers want power and how quickly the grid can expand. Grid capacity is slow to build because thousands of interconnected parts must work together, he said, which requires “deliberate study and planning” that can take years.

The industry is also rusty. After roughly 25 years of little growth in power demand, Gramlich said, utilities “got out of practice on building new infrastructure.”

Kathryn Burke, who leads U.S. specialty energy and power growth at insurance firm Marsh, told Fortune she expects around 50% to 60% of data center projects to be delayed beyond the one-to-two-year timelines developers are counting on.

Voters are pushing back on power bills

Public backlash over grid strain and rising residential electricity prices has added a second hurdle. On Nov. 3, voters rejected data center development in 40 of 41 local ballot measures, the same night Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress.

Opposition runs deepest among the young. A University of Pennsylvania Annenberg Public Policy Center survey conducted this summer found that 70% of adults under 30 oppose new data centers in their area, compared with 61% of all adults.

Voters’ fears aren’t unfounded. Northern Virginia hosts the world’s largest concentration of data centers, and Virginia sells 59% of its electricity to commercial customers, including data center clients. As of 2025, commercial energy demand exceeds residential demand in 23 states and Washington, D.C.

A study in Nature Energy by Cornell University researchers Cheng Feng and Fengqi You found that data centers raised wholesale power prices unevenly. In California’s southern Bay Area, data centers were estimated to lift wholesale prices by nearly 20% in 2025; around Dallas–Fort Worth, the increase approached 17%.

Across the four grids studied, the researchers found that data centers paid only 38% of the infrastructure costs tied to their growth in 2025: $3.12 billion of an $8.25 billion bill.

Wholesale prices make up only about 30% to 50% of a household bill, but experts say residential customers will end up covering part of the AI buildout. The Cornell researchers found the costs land hardest on lower-income and rural households, a pattern they call a “paradoxical mismatch.”

“The idea of now having to grow up and compete in terms of water prices and energy prices with a tech company is not something I can say I’m excited about,” Elijah Lee, an 18-year-old organizer with the Gen Z advocacy group Voters of Tomorrow, told Fortune before the midterms.

Big Tech is getting into the power business

Tech companies are adapting by moving into energy themselves, under a model the industry calls “bring your own power.”

Some states now require it. In August, Delaware became the first state to legislatively enact a “bring your own generation” policy, requiring large energy users such as data centers to produce or secure 100% of the power they use, including a share of clean energy, within 10 years of starting operations.

President Donald Trump’s Ratepayer Protection Pledge asks signers to “build, bring, or buy” the new-generation resources and electricity they need. Amazon, Google, Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI, Oracle and xAI signed in March, and more than 200 utilities, cooperatives, developers and Republican governors have since joined. The pledge is not binding.

On-site generation is still small but growing fast. BloombergNEF counted just 2 gigawatts of on-site gas generation operating at data centers worldwide as of March. It has since tracked 181 gigawatts of announced gas-fired generation proposed alongside data centers, more than 90% of it in the U.S.

SpaceX, for one, has proposed a roughly $24 billion supercomputing facility and gas-fired power plant at Starbase, Texas. The shift carries a climate cost: planned gas plants for data centers could raise U.S. power-sector emissions by 20%, according to a Bloomberg News analysis published by Fortune.

It isn’t a cure-all. Data center development experts say the model isn’t a long-term solution because major swings in power demand at AI data centers can cause outages and damage on-site generation equipment.

The next tests come quickly. Democrats take control of congressional committees in January. Texas Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa has proposed a moratorium on new data center development, and Ohio, which already has 125 local data center moratoriums, is set to add more.…

item.description:

Why it is here: comprehensive coverage, clear prose, and valuable context

ANTALYA, Turkey—By the time the United Nations COP31 climate talks ended Sunday afternoon, the conference center resembled a going-out-of-business sale at a pawnshop for broken dreams.

As cleaning crews cleared away the debris left by more than 100,000 participants, Murat Kurum, president of the Conference of the Parties and Turkey’s minister of environment, urbanization and climate change, tried to tie together disparate parts of a draft climate deal with a shiny ribbon of multilateralism.

Many countries were not buying it.

For the first time since 2009, the conference ended without consensus on a cover decision, the concluding statement that typically signals global solidarity on how to confront the worsening climate crisis. Countries did adopt several decisions, including a program to help workers and communities transition away from fossil fuels, and a plan to assess progress on climate adaptation.

The failure to agree on an overarching conference statement reflected deep divisions over whether the agreement should mention fossil fuels and carbon capture, as well as how much climate financing developed countries should provide to developing nations hit by costly climate disasters.

The European Union, as well as several Latin American countries and Pacific Island states, said they would not accept the proposed text from the conference leaders.

Cover decisions at the annual conferences usually focus on new steps or language that could reinforce international efforts to slow global warming. A central aim at this meeting was to set quantifiable but voluntary global goals for the widespread electrification of economies, and to increase funding from developed countries to help developing countries adapt to climate impacts.

In 2022, the U.N. conference in Egypt agreed to establish a loss and damage fund to help vulnerable countries pay for irreversible climate impacts. A year later in Dubai, delegates from more than 190 countries agreed, for the first time, that a “just and orderly” transition away from fossil fuels in energy systems is needed to slow global warming.

Since then, international collaboration on climate issues has declined amid increased conflict, rising oil and gas prices and economic insecurity. The talks in Turkey ran two days beyond the scheduled end without reaching broad agreement on potential next steps, an outcome that won’t kill the global effort but is widely viewed as a serious setback.

But compromise for the sake of consensus is not enough, said Kathy Jetn̄il-Kijiner, a climate envoy for the Marshall Islands Ministry of the Environment.

“We will not be forced to accept false solutions,” she said. “We will not compromise our future to benefit fossil fuel interests.” As written, she added, the Antalya Pact undermines her country’s security and threatens its future.

“People are dying, seas are rising and ecosystems are collapsing,” Jetn̄il-Kijiner said. “Are we so divorced from reality that we take backward steps, even as overshoot threatens to overtake us? To accept this deal would be a betrayal to the Marshallese people.”

It’s not the first time Pacific Island nations threatened by rising seas have objected to the outcome at one of the United Nations’ annual conferences. During the 2023 U.N. talks in Dubai, a final text was adopted even though a delegation representing 39 small island developing states objected because they were still outside the plenary meeting, trying to coordinate their position.

But in Antalya, the divide ran much deeper. The economically powerful and politically influential European Union, representing 28 member countries, also rejected the proposed agreement.

Ireland’s climate, energy and environment minister, Darragh O’Brien, said the European countries formally objected to the cover decision because it fell short of what the global climate crisis demands.

“We will not endorse a decision that does not even mention fossil fuels, the key driver of climate change, and not accept a COP that greenwashes fossil fuels,” said O’Brien, speaking on behalf of the EU during Ireland’s rotating presidency.

Egypt and Brazil, hosts of the U.N. climate talks in 2023 and 2025, also criticized the text proposed by COP31 president Kurum of Turkey and Chris Bowen of Australia, president of the conference negotiations.

Liliam Beatris Chagas de Moura, director for climate at Brazil’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, said she was disappointed that this year’s conference did not sustain the momentum from last year’s talks in her country.

Mohammad Ayoub, a climate negotiator with the Saudi Arabian energy ministry, said the 22-member League of Arab States supported the proposed Antalya Pact. He criticized developed countries for using up most of the global carbon budget, the amount of fossil fuels that can be burned without overheating the planet, and then asking developing countries to give up the very energy sources that fueled their own growth.

Ayoub condemned some countries’ opposition to including references to carbon dioxide removal and carbon capture and storage in the pact, calling their resistance to those technologies unscientific.

Carbon capture and storage are not close to being deployed fast enough “to keep 1.5 degrees within reach,” he said, referring to the long-term goal of limiting the average global temperature increase established by the 2015 Paris climate agreement.

“We believe that climate change requires all solutions on the table, and that countries select from these solutions depending on their national circumstances.”

item.title: The good news out of Cop31? That most of the world’s governments said no to an agreement stripped of meaning | Bill Hare
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: strong analysis, clear argument, and useful vocabulary

The failure of Cop31 in Antalya was a line in the sand moment, a victory for multiculturalism as countries stood up to the big fossil fuel producers and said no. The text they rejected barely recognised the catastrophic climate emergency we’re facing, let alone signalled a definitive move away from fossil fuels.

The good news is that most of the world’s governments rejected an agreement stripped of meaning. And the power of one particular fossil fuel producer, Saudi Arabia, needs particular scrutiny. What we also know is that co-chairing global climate talks is clearly not something to be repeated, certainly not by Australia. It didn’t work.

Governments have spent the past 35 years negotiating the global response to preventing “dangerous interference” with the climate system. Over that same period global warming has increased to close to 1.4C, with observed warming now accelerating above 0.3C per decade. Now, we’re facing an imminent breach of the Paris agreement’s critical 1.5C warming limit.

Successive Australian governments have either actively denied the problem exists – or have talked loud and long about how they are playing their role.

And what a role it has been! Australia’s coal exports have tripled since 1991; LNG exports have increased 20-fold. Australia now contributes about 4.3% of global fossil carbon emissions through both its domestic activities, and as the third-largest exporter of fossil fuels of all time.

Now that Australia’s efforts to host successful climate talks have failed so badly to deliver at a global level, we must turn to the urgent question: what will the government deliver for Australians at home?

The prime minister, Anthony Albanese, has called the current decade “critical” for combating climate change. He told leaders at Cop31 they had a “solemn responsibility” to act – and he’s said that every fraction of a degree of warming prevented matters.

If anyone needed confirmation of that during the past year, they only needed to turn on the TV news or, in some cases, to walk out of their house. From Adelaide to Sydney, the south-east broiled in January. Bush burned, homes ignited, lungs filled with smoke. Can you guess what made the heat so brutal? And the floods so powerful?

Further afield, in countries that gave the Australian colony many of its people, things were equally desperate. Italy, Greece, Britain, Spain … all of Europe crackled through its summer, leaving an estimated 50,000 people dead before their time.

South and east Asia (many of them our LNG markets) shared the pain, with temperatures hitting a close-to-unliveable 52C in Pakistan. All of it driven by climate change; all of it driven by burning fossil fuels.

So that’s the logical framing when you hear government ministers from the prime minister down celebrating new fossil fuel finds, talking about how the country benefits from extracting and exporting coal, oil and gas.

What we’re exporting is climate pain.

The government clearly didn’t turn on the TV news nor leave its house this year: it was too busy planning for coal and gas exports staying close to present levels over the next decade, at exactly the time emissions globally should be halving.

In Australia’s approvals pipeline are four “carbon bombs”, defined by scientists as projects that could emit a billion or more tonnes of fossil CO2. Off the coast of Western Australia there’s the Browse gas development at the pristine Scott Reef, the Valhalla fracking project in WA’s Kimberley further north, the Beetaloo basin fracking project in the Northern Territory, and the massive Hunter Valley Operations coalmine in New South Wales.

Albanese’s ministers have shown little other than full-blooded support for these projects going ahead. Is it no wonder then that we left Antalya with no agreement?

Rather than a decision to build on the transition away from fossil fuels (TAFF) roadmap initiated by Brazil, the only reference to fossil fuels remaining in the final text offered by Turkey was the industry’s favoured get-out-of jail-free technology – carbon capture utilisation and storage (CCUS).

The Australian government has already thrown its weight behind CCS, including special legislation to allow for offshore CO2 disposal, with virtually no evidence of its effectiveness. It is an open secret that the world’s biggest CCS project at Chevron’s Gorgon project has spectacularly failed to deliver but this has not stopped the government backing this failed technology.

We couldn’t even see the call for 35% electrification by 2035 be “clean” even with science clearly showing that if it’s not clean it will increase fossil gas use – adding a tenth of a degree of warming by mid-century.

Indeed, while the prime minister says every tenth of a degree of warming matters, his problem is that lowering every tenth of a degree of warming means his beloved gas industry loses more market share.

This week the WA premier, Roger Cook, jets off to Japan with gas giant Woodside – to talk up LNG markets.

It’s unlikely he’s going there to tell the LNG industry what’s needed to limit warming to 1.5C.

It’s also unlikely he’ll mention the International Energy Agency’s report last week showing that to limit warming to 1.5C, fossil gas demand falls by about 40% from 2025 levels by 2035, driven by rapid electrification of end-uses, efficiency improvements, and the displacement of gas-fired power generation by renewables.

Australians are looking to their federal and state governments to protect them from the terrifying ravages of climate change, yet those governments’ actions appear hyper-focused on fuelling more of it. And co-hosting the climate talks clearly didn’t help.

The government says it’s serious about climate action. By their fruits ye shall know them.

- Bill Hare, a physicist and climate scientist, is the chief executive of Climate Analytics

On Tuesday afternoon Dwayne Wilson, 69, a thin Black man dressed in a light gray prison uniform, testified about the stifling heat he experienced in the Dade correctional institute, a concrete state prison south of Miami, Florida, without air conditioning. He removed his glasses and wiped his eyes as he spoke. “It was so hot,” he said, his voice catching. “It’s so hot sometimes you have to put water on the floor just to try to keep cool.”

Wilson said he’s housed in the H dorms, a T-shaped building with one-to-two-person cells, nicknamed “hell dorm” by prisoners because its concrete walls radiate heat absorbed from the sun. The plaintiff’s law firm, the Florida Justice Institute, convinced a judge to allow 31 sensors to be temporarily installed throughout the prison during the summer of 2025. They recorded temperature and humidity levels that Stefano Shiavon, a professor of civil and environmental engineering with expertise in thermal comfort, used to calculate the heat index. He found it to be above 88F (31C) 97% of the time, with the highest heat indexes often recorded at night, including one reading in the H dorm dayroom equivalent to 119F (48C) at 10pm one July day last year. “The walls sweat,” Wilson said. “It’s miserable in the cell at night because, again, it’s so hot. No air comes to the bed we sleep at and the bed is soaked in sweat.”

Wilson is among a group of prisoners who filed a lawsuit against the Florida department of corrections in 2024 for the conditions at the Dade correctional institution, alleging that the extreme heat contributed to four deaths and has subjected prisoners to cruel and unusual punishment. The bench trial began on Monday at a federal courthouse in downtown Miami serving the US district court for the southern district of Florida. The case comes amid growing concern over extreme heat in US prisons, where more than 40 states lack statewide policies requiring prisons to provide air conditioning, even as the climate crisis drives up summer temperatures and increases the risks.

Gary Wheeler, 67, who was also housed in the H dorms at the Dade correctional institute, testified that just months ago he thought he was having a heart attack, but upon going to the medical clinic in the prison he was told by a nurse that he had heat exhaustion. “I am worried about dying. I feel like sometimes when I go to sleep at night I’m not going to wake up in the morning,” he said. “My biggest fear is if I have a heatstroke and I can’t take care of myself, I have to depend on predators who could prey on you because you’re disabled.”

Both Wheeler and Wilson submitted informal grievances to the prison about the heat in the H dorms, some dating back to at least 2019. The men talked about another inmate affected by the heat named James “Jim” Beam, who was 83 years old, wheelchair bound, and had a respiratory condition. “He would breathe like he was gasping for air,” Wheeler said. “Every time he’d breathe he would throw his head back.”

Wilson said one night he woke up when he heard Beam hollering for help from his cell across the hall from him. “It was like 2am to 3am in the morning. He was on the floor,” Wilson said. Wilson helped Beam back into his wheelchair and brought him to the medical clinic, where he was put on a breathing treatment. But a doctor ended Beam’s treatment after about 30 minutes, after which Wilson pushed him back to his cell, he said. “The vent wasn’t working in the dorm. Jim’s tongue was kind of hanging out of his mouth and he was having problems breathing,” Wilson said. Within days, Beam died.

A medical examiner’s report found Beam’s death was caused by pneumonia, but Dr Susi Vassallo, an emergency medicine physician and medical toxicologist who has served as an expert witness in several cases involving heat in US prisons, testified that she believed long-term exposure to extreme heat contributed to his death, as well as the deaths of three other prisoners at the Dade correctional institute. Vassallo said that in no other case that she has participated in has there been such extensive heat data inside the prison. “It’s rather shocking, honestly,” she said of the temperatures and humidity levels captured by the sensors in the summer of 2025. “These are dangerous heat indices, putting these individuals at substantial risk of serious harm.”

In September, a US district court judge ruled that Texas must install air conditioning in all state prisons by the end of 2029. In that case, Vassallo had testified that air conditioning was the only way to reduce the heat and related risks of illnesses and deaths.

As rain pummeled the Miami courthouse on Wednesday, Vassallo said age, certain medical conditions and specific medicines can increase the risk of heat illnesses.

During their cross-examination of expert witnesses, attorneys for the Dade correctional institute argued that more than 100 ceiling and exhaust fans throughout the facility helped mitigate heat in the prison and that the eighth amendment prohibiting “cruel and unusual punishments” was not relevant. “In 1791, when the eighth amendment was ratified, there was no air conditioning,” said Mathew Gutierrez, defense counsel for the Florida department of corrections, FDC secretary Ricky Dixon and Dade correctional institution warden Francisco Acosta, in his opening statement on Monday. “So the lack of air conditioning could not have been encompassed in the eighth amendment.” Attorneys for the defendants also said that prisoners were permitted to wear shorts and had access to water jugs with ice during the summers. But prisoners said ice in the orange water coolers quickly melted because they were filled with hot water from the showers. Vassallo said that when temperatures reach a certain point, fans aren’t helpful, and they can actually increase body temperature.…

Peter Fluck, who has died aged 85, was, with his fellow artist Roger Law, half of the Fluck & Law partnership that revived satire on TV with Spitting Image, the ITV puppet sketch show lampooning celebrities, politicians and the royal family.

Two decades after the BBC’s That Was the Week That Was spoofed the British establishment and, in particular, the last days of Harold Macmillan’s Conservative government at the time of the John Profumo affair, Spitting Image, from 1984 to 1996, mined another period of Tory rule rich in distinctive characters, exaggerating elements of their personalities.

Margaret Thatcher was portrayed as domineering, aggressive and, as time went on, increasingly tyrannical, verging on madness; Norman Tebbit as a tough thug in a leather jacket; Geoffrey Howe as dull; Nigel Lawson as incompetent and a panicker; Cecil Parkinson as a playboy; and Douglas Hurd with a Mr Whippy hairstyle.

When John Major took over as prime minister from Thatcher, he was not only represented as colourless and dull, eating peas, but physically painted grey all over.

The leaders of opposition parties, Neil Kinnock and David Steel, were treated just as cruelly, while Ronald Reagan was seen as genial, elderly and dangerous, and big names of the time – from Mick Jagger and Ian Botham to Rupert Murdoch and Laurence Olivier – made the celebrity lampooning all-embracing.

Most controversial in the early days was the inclusion of the royal family, including a gin-soaked Queen Mother, and Queen Elizabeth II always wearing a tiara, even under her headscarf.

In creating each puppet, Fluck produced a drawing from photographs, making it a recognisable caricature, before the pair developed a clay head and sculpted the facial features.

“I’m quicker when it comes to putting a likeness down on paper, but Roger Law is faster at breaking down a likeness in clay than I am,” said Fluck. “We kept turning the clay mould around on the board, switching it between us until we suddenly decided it was finished.”

From this, the puppets’ heads were cast in foam latex, with bodies mostly of foam. In front of the camera, facial features were operated by a system of wires, rods and cables devised by Fluck.

The pair met at the end of the 1950s as students at the Cambridge School of Art (now Anglia Ruskin University), where a part-time tutor was Paul Hogarth, an “artist-reporter” whose paintings and illustrations depicted events from the Spanish civil war, apartheid South Africa and other countries on his travels. He inspired in Fluck and Law an interest in political caricature.

After creating grotesque plasticine models of public figures, which were then photographed, for the Economist, the Sunday Times Magazine and others, they were approached by the graphic designer and branding expert Martin Lambie-Nairn in 1981 about bringing their characters to life on TV. Fluck and Law decided that would be best with puppets.

John Lloyd, after producing the BBC’s live-action satirical sketch show Not the Nine O’Clock News, helped to pitch what was originally titled Spit N Image to broadcasters. LWT, Thames Television, the BBC and Channel 4 all turned it down before the ITV company Central Independent Television took it on.

With Lloyd as producer, Spitting Image was launched and, after a shaky start, it captured the public’s imagination and won an International Emmy award two years running (1985 and 1986).

But it was an expensive programme to make and, by 1996, audiences had fallen from 15 to 6 million, so it was axed.

Returning to being a full-time artist and sculptor, Fluck showed no interest in being part of a Spitting Image revival for the joint ITV-BBC subscription channel BritBox in 2020, when Law returned to lead the creative team.

Born in Cambridge, to Ada (nee Hughes) and Herbert Fluck, a gardener at Magdalene College, Peter grew up birdwatching and drawing stuffed birds at the university’s Museum of Zoology. Leaving Cambridgeshire high school for boys aged 16 with “four rather miserable O-levels”, he started studying at Cambridge School of Art and reflected that Hogarth helped to guide him and Law “into the politicised 1960s”, when they marched with CND and helped with its promotional material, designing pamphlets and making woodcuts.

The pair moved to London and became freelance illustrators, with Fluck supplementing his income by teaching at Hornsey (now part of Middlesex University) and Colchester schools of art.

They then worked together on 2D and 3D plasticine models. These were photographed for publications such as Private Eye, the New Statesman, glossy magazines and newspaper colour supplements, and even seen in Germany in Stern and Der Spiegel, and the US in Time and the New York Times.

In 1976, the year in which they formalised their partnership as Fluck & Law, working from a defunct temperance mission hall in Cambridge, they produced a Radio Times front cover of an “all-American family”, including dog, engrossed watching television to promote programmes marking the American bicentennial.

Following the end of Spitting Image, Fluck moved to Cornwall and, living in a cliff-top house in a fishing village, worked and exhibited as an artist whose creations included mobiles, ceramics, interactive installations and sculptural pieces.

In 1963, Fluck married Anne-Cécile de Bruyne. She and their son and daughter survive him.

In the titular story of Georgi Gospodinov’s short-story collection The Man With Many Names, the narrator reveals: “Telling our personal stories is the only move we can make … that allows us to postpone for at least a little while this game’s foregone ending.” It’s as good a description as any of the Bulgarian author’s preoccupation with stories and their power to upset life’s linear course. Like his idol Jorge Luis Borges, Gospodinov tends towards subversion in his fiction: he takes the “game” and rewrites the rules, turns the board upside down to find new ways of looking and seeing. If the ending is a foregone conclusion, Gospodinov’s magic is to make his stories feel like beginnings with endless possibilities.

The Man With Many Names comprises 40 stories made up of two collections previously published in Bulgarian. Ranging from post-Communist realism to experimental fables set in unfamiliar worlds, these magnificently imaginative pieces trade in many of the same themes – childhood, the labyrinthine qualities of language, the push and pull of fantasy and reality – as his best-known work, Time Shelter, for which he won the International Booker prize in 2023, shared with translator Angela Rodel, who also translated this collection. Here too Rodel expertly conveys Gospodinov’s economy of language, as well as his playfulness and warmth as a storyteller.

One of Gospodinov’s charming quirks is his tendency to speak directly to the reader, orienting them within the apparatus of the story. So let’s dive in, as he would say. One of the collection’s most affecting stories is Blind Vaysha (adapted into an Oscar-nominated animation by Theodore Ushev), the tale of a girl who with one eye sees into the future and with the other into the past. The trick is that Gospodinov turns Vaysha’s “blindness” into a more universal problem, as if to say we all see like Vaysha in some way.

Other standout stories in this fabular vein include The Christmas Soul of a Pig, in which a pig meditates on life, death, hypocrisy, and religion as he is prepped for slaughter; And Everything Became Moon, about a man who chooses the day of his death through a special government department; Eight Minutes and Nineteen Seconds, in which a world-renowned judge of sunsets returns to his home town to witness the apocalypse. In this story, we also bear witness to the molten core of Gospodinov’s outward morbidity; the sun has gone out, we have eight minutes to live, so what else is there to do but admire the beauty of a sunset?

Another persistent theme of the collection is love-that-cannot-be: missed connections, unfulfilled reunions. In Peonies and Forget-Me-Nots, one of the collection’s best stories, two strangers meet at an airport and fall in love. They accept they cannot be together, so invent a life of shared memories instead. After they part, the man returns home to his wife and can’t explain “what he’d been doing during those 50 years when he’d been gone” – as if their little game had bent the laws of time. Part of the pleasure of reading Gospodinov is the force of his imagination, which feels as insistently real as a child’s. This story mirrors Oh, Henry!, where two young lovers travel to each other’s home towns on Christmas Eve as a surprise, only to realise they both, tragically, had the same idea.

This twist on O Henry’s 1905 classic The Gift of the Magi is one of many literary hints that Gospodinov drops. There are stories that recall the psychological noir of Paul Auster, the literary gamesmanship of Vladimir Nabokov and the political acerbism of Milan Kundera (all three are referenced in the collection). And saturating everything he writes, the inventiveness of Borges. In the afterword, Gospodinov modestly describes “Borges and my grandmother” as his two key influences.

But Gospodinov’s world-building also has its own private logic, and in these stories we wade through the flotsam of his familiar inventory: trains (in A Second Story, A Station Story, Christine Waving from the Train and Daughter), ears and their potential dismemberment (in Forging the Bulgarian Earring, In Front of Hotel Bulgaria, and Six Degrees of Separation), the figure of the Minotaur (in The Eighth Night), cinema, Russian literature, flowers, pickles, ghosts, and dreary editorial offices. One final word must go to Gaustine, an elusive, shapeshifting character who is never far from view in Gospodinov’s works; readers may remember him as the psychiatrist in Time Shelter, and he appears in several of these stories. It is to him we are indebted for the idea above that “stories will always put off the end”, Gospodinov reveals, as well as other witty and wise interjections throughout. Hats off to Gaustine, and hats off to Gospodinov for telling us these stories while we postpone the ending.

How much do you earn? If the question makes you bristle – and I realise we haven’t even met – would you answer it if someone convinced you that your candour might just change the world?

In her deliciously original first book, the former Guardian data journalist and illustrator Mona Chalabi sets out to do precisely that. The result – a dazzling mix of journalism, data visualisation and memoir – is both a joy to read and a serious provocation. Chalabi takes aim at our silence and furtiveness around individual income and finances. “Our collective ignorance is sustaining an unfair system,” she argues. Unless we talk more openly about our personal wealth, we will never be able to tackle the economic problems causing insecurity and anxiety for us all.

Ten Lives is a riveting exemplar of financial transparency. It tells the stories of 10 individual Americans, exploring how their wealth – or lack of it – has shaped every aspect of their lives. There is Jacob, the New York investment banker earning more than half a million dollars a year who uses an elastic band as a wallet, for fear of squandering money. There is former teen gambling addict Levi, now trying to rebuild his life in his 20s, whose greatest concern about being interviewed is the shame of appearing broke. There is grad student Kristina, newly divorced and forced to choose between finishing her degree and raising her child. Her solution is surrogacy. Being paid to grow someone else’s baby is the only way she can expand her options for childcare and, as a result, for her life.

Chalabi chose her subjects, whom she followed closely over a five-year period, to represent us all. In her introduction, she asks us to imagine lining up every person in the US from the poorest to the richest, then dividing that line into 10 equally sized groups. Each interviewee comes from one of those groups, or deciles, meaning all 10 steps on the US income ladder are depicted. Jacob is 10th decile (household income more than $272,000), Kristina is fifth ($59,000–$75,000) and Levi is third ($35,000–$46,000).

And then there is the 11th subject: Chalabi herself. Leading by example, she reveals the size of her advance for this book ($850,000 – or, in her terms, a “shitload of money”), provides a spreadsheet of her freelance earnings for the same five-year period as her subjects, and admits to having been able to buy a five-bedroom home in London for more than £1.5m. Her candour extends to revealing her discomfort as an advocate for social justice who has become, undeniably, rich. “If we rise too far, there’s a risk we will become the very thing we have criticised,” she admits.

Frankness is Chalabi’s signature trait. The words and illustrations that make up this book are an exhilarating antidote to obfuscation and evasiveness of every kind. She loathes all “word smush” that disguises reality, and her own prose is succinct, blunt and sinewy. Take, for example, her withering criticism of George Orwell for conducting a narcissistic poverty safari with Down and Out in Paris and London. The book is an example, she believes, of “class cosplay”, written by “a rich boy who changed his clothing and, presumably, his accent, to pass as a ‘tramp’”.

Considering its bedrock is hard numerical data, Ten Lives is a deeply affecting book. Her subjects’ stories reveal how easily systemic problems such as lack of affordable healthcare or childcare can overturn lives in modern America. Chalabi herself has to pour her savings into paying for care for her mother after she suffers a debilitating stroke in the UK. What unites all 11 of them is a gnawing fear for their financial futures – irrespective of how much they earn. The corrosive individualism of advanced capitalism supercharges these fears, argues Chalabi, by indoctrinating us into a belief that “we cannot support one another or be supported when we need to be.” But this is patently untrue. The world is not entirely dog-eat-dog. We can and do lean on family, friends and communities when we need to. We help each other out because we are care – and we are far from driven by avarice alone.

Chalabi concludes that what is needed to feel financially secure – and therefore to free ourselves from the treadmill of acquisition – is a proper societal safety net. A well-funded government, in other words, that spends enough on healthcare, education and welfare. To get there, instead of railing impotently at Bezos and Musk and the rest of the ultra-rich elite, we could start by being more open about how much wealth we have – and how much we owe and rely on each other. Otherwise, we will all remain in the dark, unsure, unprotected, afraid. It’s a brilliant, radical argument, delivered with ingenuity and panache.

Why it is here: original reporting, evidence and concrete detail

With his twinkling eyes and silver ponytail, M John Harrison doesn’t seem anything like his 81 years. The M stands for Michael, Mike to his friends. And last night he became the oldest author to win the Booker prize for fiction, for his 13th novel, The End of Everything. Our interview is delayed because of wifi issues, which is fitting given that the novel is about – among many things – what happens when non-human intelligence takes over.

The End of Everything is the first sci-fi novel to have won the prize in its 58-year history, which is almost as long as Harrison has been writing. “It’s interesting,” he replies, when asked if he feels vindicated, “that something that has an SF-adjacent feel can be regarded as a serious book and given the Booker prize. My problem has always been that I don’t believe in genre. I don’t believe in it in any way.” He gently wags his finger at me. It is a bit like having coffee with a cheerier, more neatly bearded Gandalf – it will surprise no one that, in his youth, Harrison read The Lord of the Rings every year for a decade.

Whether he likes it or not, Harrison is hailed as a titan of literary science fiction. His fans have included giants such as the late Ursula K Le Guin and Iain Banks, as well as China Miéville today, and more surprisingly the Sex and the City star, and last year’s Booker judge, Sarah Jessica Parker. But he is not, as he would be the first to say, a household name. Although that has been changing. In 2020 he won the Goldsmiths prize for The Sunken Land Begins to Rise Again, and in 2022 he was himself a Booker judge.

The End of Everything took around 15 years to write, with real-world events overtaking him. AI, late capitalism, environmental collapse, the refugee crisis, Brexit – nearly all the manifestations of today’s omni-crisis can be found in the pages of this slim, elusive novel. As its title suggests, this is the work for our end times. “I suddenly thought, ‘Well, you’re 80, you might as well have a go at pushing it over the cliff one more time.’ My rule has always been push it as far as it will go, then move back slightly from the edge. But this time I thought, ‘Let’s push it over and see what happens.’”

And what happens is anyone’s guess. As critics have pointed out, The End of Everything deliberately resists definition. It is a triumph of obfuscation. “I could explain some of it to you,” the author says tantalisingly. “But no, I don’t want to.” For Harrison, the world ends not with a bang, but with endless confusion. “It was a book designed to present the explanatory collapse and epistemological collapse that you see in societies that have suddenly lost their grounding.”

He describes it as a mix of gothic horror, road movie, science fiction and fantasy – even “a seaside novel”. I would add satire to the list. One thing it is not, Harrison is clear, is a dystopia, but rather a post-disaster novel in the tradition of early JG Ballard or John Wyndham. But he wanted to play with the conventions; he didn’t want the reader to know more than the characters. “It would be ordinary sci-fi,” he says, “if you were told it was the triffids.”

Set in an unnamed coastal town somewhere in Kent (“If this is hell, it looks a lot like Margate,” as Peaky Blinders famously had it) in the nearish future, The End of Everything depicts a disintegrating Britain, after an invasion by an alien species called the iGhettis, which appear as “tall writhing bursts of light”. The iGhettis are a play on “I get it” (explanation), “I get stuff” (capitalism), Getty (extreme wealth), Apple (tech), I (Freud). “I wrote it down and I thought, ‘This is cheap.’ And then I looked at it again and thought, ‘Oh my God, there are so many ambiguities packed into that one word,’” he says with glee.

The germ of the novel was the financial crisis of 2007-8. “I had the rage, but I couldn’t make it work.” So he put what he had written away in a drawer and in 2015 “cannibalised” it for a short story called The Crisis. It was almost the end of him. During a reading of the story at an event in east London, he was struck by what felt like the worst indigestion of his life. “I thought, ‘That’ll teach you to down two glasses of red wine and eat pizza before performing.’” Two days later he was taken to hospital and told he’d had a heart attack. He was just shy of 70. When he returned to The Crisis, he realised it was the blueprint for a whole novel. “I was like, ‘Wow!’ And began to work on it.”

Harrison was born in Rugby, Warwickshire, in 1945. The closeness of the second world war overshadowed his childhood. “You were never allowed to forget it.” His father was an engineer, and the family lived on an estate of modern houses built for postwar key workers. One of the defining memories of his childhood was a Narnia-style wardrobe that, when he climbed into it, “was a library of trash novels” from 1920s thrillers to contemporary sci-fi magazines.

“It was full of all the things you weren’t supposed to enjoy,” he says with delight. He doesn’t know who the books belonged to. His parents had a very small bookcase with some classics downstairs in the lounge. “But it was the most extraordinary education for the imagination.” His father died when he was 13 and his mother never got over his death, something Harrison will explore if he ever writes his autobiography.

When he was 21, he published his first short story in the science-fiction magazine Science Fantasy. He became literary editor of New Worlds in 1968. He had a number of odd jobs – a groom at a hunting stables, a clerk, a trainee teacher. “Being a kind of hippy, I decided that if you were going to write, you would only write, and that you would take the consequences,” he says. That meant couch-surfing and often not having much to eat. “We were all living in appalling circumstances in west London before west London was west London,” he says of his fellow writers. “And it was great fun.”…

Wendell Berry on Where Our Gone Loved Ones Go

To love is to sign a contract with loss. To love anyway is both the great tragedy and the great triumph of life.

When two people have loved one another, each has become embedded in the marrow of the other’s being and both have had a profound experience that cannot be unhad even when the slender thread of grace between them is severed, by death or disenchantment. “No one you love is ever dead,” Hemingway wrote in his moving meditation on death and the meaning of life disguised as a letter of consolation to a bereaved friend.

Death, of course, is only one species of loss, one way our loved ones can leave us. We can also be left in life, left behind, left wondering where love goes when it goes. At its most discomposing, abandonment can feel like a living death.

All deep loss has one thing in common: It opens an absence so acutely felt it kidnaps us from presence, takes us away from our own lives and their insistent, inconvenient, sacred ongoingness. In memory or in fantasy, we end up refugees from reality, ceding the only thing that is ever ours for the keeping: the living moment. In all missing, we miss life.

That is what the achingly missed Wendell Berry (August 5, 1934–August 31, 2026) explores in this gasp of a poem, originally published in the November 17, 2025 issue of The New Yorker:

THE LOVED ONES

by Wendell Berry

The loved ones we call the dead

depart from us and for a while are absent. And then as if

called back by our love, they come

near us again. They enter our dreams.

We feel they have been near us

when we have not thought of them.

They are simply here, simply waiting

while we are distracted among

our obligations. At last

it comes to us: They live now

in the permanent world.

We are the absent ones.

Couple with physicist Richard Feynman’s extraordinary love letter to his wife written long after her untimely death, then revisit Wendell Berry on creativity and love and his timeless antidote to despair.

The Relationship Between Comedy, Democracy, and AI

“Humor, more than anything else in the human make-up, can afford an aloofness and an ability to rise above any situation, even if only for a few seconds,” Viktor Frankl wrote in recalling the role of humor as a lifeline to sanity and survival in the Holocaust.

Humor is a fundamental human freedom: To laugh is to protect ourselves from all that dehumanizes us — tyranny and transactionalism, captivity and commodification. Humor is also fundamental to free societies, to freedom of thought, to democracy: To laugh together is to harmonize our deepest humanity.

Because humor is the art of surprise, it exists beyond the reach of — and is an antidote to — the artifices of predictive computation we mistake for intelligence.

In her altogether fantastic manifesto for breaking free from the prison of predictive technologies, Carissa Véliz argues that humor thrives in the same “spaces of indeterminacy” where creativity and innovation also thrive. (“Whatever inspiration is, it’s born from a continuous ‘I don’t know,’” the Polish poet Wisława Szymborska observed in her magnificent Nobel Prize acceptance speech.) With an eye to the emotional attunement of sharing laughter, Véliz considers the relationship between humor, democracy, and AI:

Our sense of humor is a dialogue, and when we delegate the conversation to AI, we lose the personal relationship with another human being. Democracy itself is a conversation. If we give up our seat at that table and give it to an AI, we will lose our voice.

Comedy is not inconsequential for democracy. Comedy sets the tone for freedom. It gives us courage. A documentary about comedy clubs in war-torn Ukraine reminds me that humor is not a luxury; it’s indispensable. “When I went to Sarajevo to a film festival,” Cleese says, “people were talking about the early ’90s, when Yugoslavia was falling apart. Sarajevo is down in a valley, and the Serbs were up in the hills throwing shells down, and telescopic snipers were shooting people crossing the street. And they told me that they had found an underground car park, had turned it into a cinema, and they would show comedies, including Monty Python, and they would laugh. When they came out, an hour and a half later, they felt better. Nothing had improved. But they were better able to deal with their situation.” Comedy can be an ally in our challenge to defy the odds.

Humor, like creativity, works by defying expectation. It is a felicitous violation of the norm. Societies thrive and progress by continually challenging the norm, the given, the status quo. Every revolution, every change in regime, is the story of turning the old order from terrible to laughable.

The Generosity of Selfishness: C.S. Lewis on How to Be Interesting

Our lives are defined not by what we have but what we give — on what and whom we spend our energy and time, how we share our material possessions and our mental powers, what we do with our gifts. “Anything you do not give freely and abundantly becomes lost to you,” Annie Dillard wrote in contemplating the nature of creativity. “You open your safe and find ashes.”

Paradoxically, the ability to give hinges on the ability to receive: You must be rested in order to labor, taking the repose it takes to recharge your vital energies; you must be interested in order to be interesting, taking the world in with a greedy curiosity that absorbs its beauty and strangeness in order to metabolize it into meaning.

C.S. Lewis (November 29, 1898–November 22, 1963) offers a wonderfully counterintuitive perspective on our notions of generosity and our ideas about what it means to be interesting in his memoir Surprised by Joy (public library).

With an eye to the ideal structure of the creative life, he writes:

It is a life almost entirely selfish. Selfish, not self-centred: for in such a life my mind would be directed towards a thousand things, not one of which is myself. The distinction is not unimportant. One of the happiest men and most pleasing companions I have ever known was intensely selfish. On the other hand I have known people capable of real sacrifice whose lives were nevertheless a misery to themselves and to others, because self-concern and self-pity filled all their thoughts. Either condition will destroy the soul in the end. But till the end, give me the man who takes the best of everything (even at my expense) and then talks of other things, rather than the man who serves me and talks of himself, and whose very kindnesses are a continual reproach, a continual demand for pity, gratitude, and admiration.

This is also why, Lewis intimates, the “thrill” of our greatest creative breakthroughs — those revelations that give us back to ourselves, out of which we give our best work to the world — is rooted in “self-forgetfulness”:

Only when your whole attention and desire are fixed on something else — whether a distant mountain, or the past, or the gods of Asgard — does the “thrill” arise.

[…]

Shut your mouth; open your eyes and ears. Take in what is there.

Couple with John Steinbeck on the art of receiving, then revisit C.S. Lewis on what we long for in our existential longing.

item.description:

Suzanne Collins never had to invent a word for the country at the center of The Hunger Games: she borrowed one. Panem is Latin for "bread," with Roman ties, and the same word used for "daily bread" in the Latin Lordâs Prayer.

On its own, it's a fitting name for a nation where kids go hungry, but Collins took the word out of a much nastier sentence.

Bread and Circuses

Around the year 100 CE, the Roman poet Juvenal wrote his 10th satire, a long, sour poem about how badly people choose what to wish for, and partway through it he takes a swing at his fellow citizens. "Romeâs voters once handed out military commands and consulships," he complains, "but now theyâve stopped caring about any of it": in G.G. Ramsayâs 1918 translation, the public âlongs eagerly for just two things,â bread and games. In Latin, the two things are panem et circenses, and Mental Floss has counted the phrase among the Latin you should be using.

Juvenal wasnât being abstract: Rome really did hand out free grain to its citizens, and the cityâs magistrates gave out tokens called tesserae that could be exchanged for a fixed amount of grain or money. Panem has its own tesserae: a kid in the districts can sign up for one in exchange for a yearâs supply of grain and oil, and the price is one more slip with their name on it in the reaping bowl.

Plutarch Explains the Joke

The translation comes in Mockingjay, the third novel, when Plutarch Heavensbee, the former Head Gamemaker, tells Katniss itâs âa saying from thousands of years ago, written in a language called Latin about a place called Rome.â As he puts it, âThe writer was saying that in return for full bellies and entertainment, his people had given up their political responsibilities and therefore their power.â

Collins has said the bread in her books cuts both ways. Asked in an interview for the seriesâ 10th anniversary why she made Peeta a baker, she said that when he throws a starving Katniss a loaf, âheâs keeping her alive long enough to work out a strategy for survival,â which made him âa life giver.â But, she added, âthereâs a dark side to bread, too. When Plutarch Heavensbee references it, heâs talking about Panem et Circenses, Bread and Circuses, where food and entertainment lull people into relinquishing their political power.â

A Capitol Full of Romans

Panem isnât the only Roman name Collins borrowed. Plutarch is named for the biographer Plutarch, whose Lives Collinsâs father used to read to her: when Spartacus came on TV, heâd get out the âLife of Crassus,â since Spartacus, a slave, âdidnât rate his own book.â And in The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes, the District 2 boy Sejanus Plinth is named for Lucius Aelius Sejanus, who rose to enormous power under the emperor Tiberius and was executed for conspiring against him.

That last one ties back to Juvenal, who wrote his âbread and circusesâ line in the middle of a scene about the real Sejanusâs fall. In Ramsayâs translation, his statues come down, the head of âthe darling of the mobâ goes into the furnace and comes out as frying pans and slop pails, and âSejanus is being dragged along by a hook, as a show and joy to all!â The same crowd, Juvenal says, would have hailed Sejanus as emperor if things had gone the other way, because it âfollows fortune, as it always does, and rails against the condemned.â A public execution staged as a show for a crowd that cheers whoeverâs winning is about as Panem as it gets, and it was sitting right next to the name the whole time.

A cannibalistic nightmare: the terrifying ordeal of the Donner Party

In 1846, a group of families left the American Midwest in search of a new life in California – but one disastrous shortcut left them fighting for their lives. Jonny Wilkes tells the harrowing story of the Donner Party

The 19th century brought monumental change to the landscape of the United States. As the still-fledgling nation acquired more territory, more American eyes began to look out across the vast continent and envisage a better life in the west. The Oregon Territory and California, then part of Mexico, promised prosperity, freedom and a fresh start, inspiring pioneering migrants to brave the difficult and dangerous journey to carve out their own slice of paradise there.

Driving this westward expansion was ‘manifest destiny’ – the belief that it was the God-given right and duty of the US to extend its borders to the Pacific Ocean and beyond. That phrase first appeared in 1845; the very next year, a group of would-be settlers set out along the recently established Oregon Trail to realise that dream. Instead, they endured a nightmare, created from a catalogue of errors and misfortunes. Their name evokes a macabre chapter in US history: the Donner Party.

The Reeds and the Donners

The doomed party began with two large families from Illinois who joined the wave of humanity to California. There were the Reeds, headed by Irish-born businessman James Reed, and the Donners, led by farming brothers George and Jacob Donner. Accompanying them were their wives, children, servants and teamsters to drive the wagons, as well as cattle and horses.

In an intriguing ‘what-if’, a bright young lawyer by the name of Abraham Lincoln seriously considered going too. The future president, a friend of Reed’s, was talked out of it by his wife Mary Todd, and turned his attentions to his political career instead.

On 14 April 1846, the Reeds and Donners set out from Springfield, Illinois, bound for Independence, Missouri, the starting point of the great trails to the west. The town provided them with the opportunity to stock up and attach themselves to a wagon train for the 2,000-plus-mile journey, which usually took four to six months.

When they left Independence on 12 May, it was already late in the migration season: it was important to go late enough to avoid the rains and mud of spring, while ensuring plenty of grass for the cattle, but early enough to beat the snow.

Aware of the time pressure, they covered the ground to Fort Laramie (now in Wyoming) by late June with little incident, except for the death of Reed’s elderly and sickly mother-in-law, Sarah Keyes. From there, migrants tended to turn north to Fort Hall either to carry on with the Oregon Trail or join the California Trail. Most of the wagon train kept to the established track.

George Donner, however, took the lead of a breakaway group, which included the Reeds as well as the Breen, Eddy, Murphy, McCutchen and Keseberg families, and later the Graves family too. The so-called Donner Party numbered 87 people, nearly half of whom were children.

The shortcut

The party decided to take a new route, known as the Hastings Cutoff. An explorer named Lansford Hastings had written a book, The Emigrants’ Guide to Oregon and California, in which he promoted a shortcut he had devised. Instead of going north and around the Great Salt Lake, he suggested trekking over the Wasatch Mountains and straight across the Great Salt Lake Desert, apparently saving more than 350 miles.

In reality, the Hastings Cutoff added around 125 miles and Hastings had never traversed the route in its entirety, let alone gauged its suitability for wagons and cattle. Yet he sent out letters offering to guide migrants, which is how he enticed members of the Donner Party.

Reed even ignored warnings by an old friend not to trust Hastings, while another traveller, journalist Edwin Bryant, wrote his own letters warning against the use of the shortcut, but these went undelivered. The proprietor of a trading post – who stood to profit from use of the Hastings Cutoff – managed to hide the letters, and instead told the party to expect a smooth road.

What they found was nearly impassable terrain and no Hastings to help them. He had gone ahead to guide another group, so the Donner Party relied on instructions left along the way. They forged a path through the wilderness, clearing the brush, stones and trees, and dragged their wagons up the steep mountains. At their slowest, they progressed just 1.5 miles a day, causing them to fall behind schedule.

Banished from the party

When the party reached the Great Salt Lake Desert, an arid expanse of salt flats without water or grass, they found a note from Hastings claiming it would take two days to cross. In the end, it took five, with the days baking hot, the nights painfully cold, and every step hindered as the wagons sank in the sticky crust of the desert. Supplies ran low, wagons had to be abandoned, many cattle died or fled, and everyone was exhausted by the time they reached the other side.

They did not get to the Humboldt River, where they reconnected with the well-trodden trail to California, until late September. The Hastings Cutoff delayed them by a month and so raised serious doubts over whether they could cross the Sierra Nevada mountains before the snows fell. Morale, energy and supplies plummeted, and cattle numbers dwindled in raids from local Native American tribes. Four deaths came in quick succession, including an old man left on the road when he could go no further.…

item.title: I’m a priest. Silicon Valley’s search for the ‘soul’ of AI is deeply troubling | Rev Kevin Deal
item.description:

Why it is here: substance, clear and thought-provoking

Last month, religious leaders from across San Francisco gathered behind closed doors to discuss what it means to be human in the age of artificial intelligence.

Anthropic, the AI company operating only a couple of miles from my parish, has been courting priests, rabbis and theologians. Its billionaire cofounder, Christopher Olah, has even pressed Vatican advisers to take seriously the possibility that his company’s chatbot might possess consciousness.

As a priest, I find this pursuit deeply troubling. I welcome serious conversations about AI’s moral implications, especially theological ones. But the extraordinary effort to establish whether a machine might have consciousness, or possess a soul, reveals a profound misunderstanding of what makes us human.

Our souls and minds and bodies are so much more than the tasks we perform.

We as humans make mistakes, sometimes catastrophic ones, and then we may or may not try to correct course. We may double down in stubbornness, insisting on our rightness. We express ourselves, connect with others, reproduce, indulge, purge; we strive toward a goal, transform in an encounter, make vows, renege them, encounter the void, try to fill it, fail, drown out the dread, and go about the humdrum tasks of everyday life as honestly as we can.

From a young age, we are nurtured and protected by our caregivers. We experience beauty and sit with mysteries. We do not exist merely for utility.

Artificial intelligence could never replicate the transcendent mundanity of who we are. Even if every synapse in our brains were externally replicated, even if the perfect AI configuration were designed to duplicate our central nervous system, it would still lack divine spark.

Artificial intelligence is formed as commerce, pure utility. Its existence requires enormous concentrations of capital, infrastructure, and the accumulated intelligence of humanity. It’s an ongoing economic choice, driven by pursuit of profit, hope for a better world, and sociopolitical fear. If a model doesn’t make a good return, it’s cast aside.

Whatever the sincere hopes of its creators, AI is being developed within an economic system that increasingly measures the worth of everything solely by its productivity. That is what makes Silicon Valley’s fascination with the spirituality of its machines so strange.

Its founders are turning to religious leaders to ask whether their creations might possess consciousness, how they might be taught goodness, even whether they should learn to confess their wrongdoings.

Yet the very traditions they are consulting have spent millennia teaching us that goodness cannot be reduced to a set of behaviors, any more than the soul of humanity, as magnificent and ineffable as it is, can be replicated by a machine.

And while Silicon Valley seeks to establish the humanity of its products, it seems increasingly comfortable treating actual human beings as little more than instruments of production.

Consider confession, a practice Anthropic researchers have reportedly considered teaching their models. In Christianity, confession demands more than acknowledging a mistake or expressing regret. It requires us to confront the harm we’ve caused, seek forgiveness, and strive to change how we live.

If Silicon Valley’s founders want to learn from this tradition, they might begin by asking what they themselves have to confess about the technologies they’re unleashing upon the world.

So how do we counter this impoverished vision of humanity?

Well, I have a radical suggestion for all of us, but especially the tech billionaires searching for answers in Christianity.

Go to church.

Choose one rooted in the ancient and mysterious practices of the faith. Lean into the practice of the faith and the sacraments, attend mass, confess, and pray daily. Read the scriptures, find spiritual mentors, struggle with belief, make new friends, and forgive old ones.

If you stop trying to be effective and instead strive to be good – that is, to be truly human, reflecting God’s light – you will be surprised by the joy that enters into the depths of your soul.

In the sacraments, prayers, beauty and mystery of the liturgy, and the shared life of faith, we encounter a vision of humanity that resists the relentless demand to be useful. We receive the body of Christ and strive to become more like him. We turn toward a world where justice and mercy kiss, where renewal and forgiveness are continually possible.

When you leave church, carry those teachings back to your offices and boardrooms. Ask how the decisions you make affect the poor, the workers whose livelihoods are being transformed, and the neighbors who will never share in your wealth.

The mystery of the Christian faith is inseparable from its demands upon how we live. You cannot claim to embrace its wisdom while setting aside the obligations it places upon you.

Human worth is not rooted in what we produce, and our minds were not created to be quarried for profit. We were created, in the words of Jesus and all the prophets, to love God and our neighbors.

The great moral question facing Silicon Valley is not whether its machines can become more like us. It is whether the people building them are willing to treat the rest of humanity as something more than machines.

- The Rev Kevin Deal is the priest at St John the Evangelist Episcopal church in San Francisco

item.title: The Guardian view on Grand Theft Auto VI: a game that makes players think twice | Editorial
item.description:
