Why it is here: substance, thought-provoking

The biggest global cultural event of the year may not be something that millions of people watch together but somewhere that millions of people venture separately. In the video game Grand Theft Auto VI, players inhabit a fictionalised America through the eyes of two lovers turned cons in a rags-to-riches crime epic. On Thursday, when the game was released, workers called in sick and students skipped lectures to play at home. Such is GTA VI’s appeal that it is forecast to rake in billions of dollars within months.

The game has been billed as a satire of American capitalism, and it is undoubtedly a landmark in interactive storytelling and art. The commercial success of its previous titles has rivalled that of Hollywood blockbusters. Playing GTA VI, as the Guardian’s video games editor observes, is like losing yourself in a doorstop novel, with hours of solitary immersion in a vividly conjured place – not a facsimile of modern Miami, but an interpretation, almost the size of Manchester, rendered with astonishing precision by the artists who designed, wrote, coded and soundtracked its virtual world.

The video game portrays a country awash with vice and hypocrisy, where the American dream is alive and well – provided you trample on someone else to achieve it. There is no way to win if you play by the rules. In the game’s main hub, Vice City, lawyers and police are scarcely more honest than drug dealers and thieves, while conspiracy theorists, crypto scammers and narcissistic influencers abound. But it would be wrong to think that the game simply revels in corruption. By giving its two main characters, Jason and Lucia, histories and vulnerabilities, the game asks players to sympathise with people who are both society’s victims and its perpetrators.

The GTA series has long faced criticism for its violence and casual misogyny, treating women as sex objects or punchlines. GTA VI marks a shift. Lucia, its first female lead, confronts the sexism around her, while other women emerge as characters in their own right. Even the violence, reviews suggest, feels less gratuitous. The game portrays a Trumpian America where wealth, spectacle and criminality blend together. But its satire no longer relies quite so heavily on making women its targets.

Why is one of the most culturally important depictions of the US a fantasy in which the American dream can be pursued most freely by breaking the law? This is a question that hangs over GTA VI. It was created by a team of 5,000 people, many of whom are based outside the US (Rockstar, the company behind the game, is headquartered in Scotland). This is an America created largely by outsiders. But then, as one of Rockstar’s lead developers Rob Nelson said: “We’re all outsiders to this version of America.”

Mr Nelson thinks that the game’s real innovation may not be the scale of the world that Rockstar has built, but the morally complex relationship that its developers have created between the player and this imagined world. Reviewers remark on behaving more considerately while playing the game, and how it rewards attentiveness in some of its fictional relationships and encourages players to talk their way out of trouble rather than immediately reaching for a gun. After decades of allowing players to behave badly online with impunity, GTA VI doesn’t necessarily want them to be good, but it asks them to think twice about being bad.

Why it is here: substance, interesting perspective

The sun has set on Orlando, Florida, the theme-park capital of the world. Inside one of those parks, Walt Disney World’s EPCOT, thousands of visitors make their way toward a manmade lagoon surrounded by pavilions representing cultures and histories from around the world. Of the many times that I have visited Disney World with my family, some of my favourite moments have come at this point in our trip, while we prepare for EPCOT’s fireworks display to begin. My daughter is generally sitting in her mobility chair as the rest of the family debriefs about the day’s activities, our legs tired from all the time we’ve spent on our feet. The temperature has usually cooled off a bit, and the collective nature of the experience is palpable. Around us, families and groups of friends are huddled together, anticipating the start of the show.

As lights begin to flash around the water, an opening narration sets the tone for what’s to come:

Everyone on this Earth is part of the great Symphony of Us. Each of us a unique instrument playing harmony to one another. And even though we are all playing different parts, it’s our unified heartbeat that connects us, reminding us that we are more alike than we are different. A rhapsody of rhythms that unites us and connects us through commonalities of the heart.

It’s high-minded, sentimental stuff for a theme park with rides featuring a talking snowman and a rat who becomes a chef. But at a time of rising scepticism about multiculturalism and universal values, it’s also a message that has come to resonate with me.

Like many families, we have formed meaningful memories at Disney World because of the entertainment-rich environment the Disney company has created. Its theme parks are enjoyable, in part, because they appeal to each member of my family. But our Disney memories are also meaningful because Disney World reflects my values: this is a place that is ostensibly committed to the idea that we are all, in some sense, citizens of the world bound together by a common humanity. It’s a simple ideal. But it’s one I believe in deeply and strive to embody, however imperfectly, in my life.

Of course, as a philosopher, I’m also keenly aware that all the experiences that have led to these moments at Disney World have been sold to me by a massive global corporation that strives to maximise its profits. Whether the Walt Disney Company genuinely believes in the cosmopolitan values it promotes is largely beside the point. What matters is whether portraying those values is a good business strategy. Disney is also a corporation that has received more than its share of criticism throughout its history. It has been criticised for its labour practices, for the cultural themes in its films, for the stands it takes (or does not take) on controversial public issues and, sometimes, simply for being a massive global corporation that strives to maximise its profits. This tension regularly leaves me puzzled. Is the value of my experience at Disney World undermined by the fact that it is, at the end of the day, a production of the Walt Disney Company? Can I trust a profit-hungry corporation to teach my children universal values? And does Disney’s message need to be sincere for it to really matter?

These sorts of questions are certainly not unique to Disney theme parks. In his book The Affluent Society (1958), the economist John Kenneth Galbraith coined the term ‘the dependence effect’ to characterise the process by which a business creates the desires that it seeks to satisfy. For example, you might not have wanted to buy a new sweater, but seeing a commercial on television makes you dissatisfied with your current wardrobe such that you hop online and order a new one. It likely never occurred to you to try iced tea with vodka until you saw the beverage advertised in a magazine, but now you find yourself on the way to the corner store to buy a six-pack. And Disney obviously wants to manufacture the desire to visit its theme parks because it will make money from everyone who wants to satisfy their newfound urge to ride Frozen Ever After and take pictures of their kids with Mickey and Minnie. For Galbraith, the dependence effect is problematic because it gives too much control over our lives to people who simply want to make money.

While contemporary critics of Disney might echo these concerns, the problem becomes more acute when the corporation in question has behaved poorly in other ways. The Walt Disney Company has long been the target of labour activists who criticise how Disney treats its employees. In 2024, unionised workers at Disneyland authorised a strike in contract negotiations where they argued that 73 per cent of their employees didn’t make enough money to cover basic living expenses, despite often working 12- to 14-hour days. That strike was ultimately averted, but it stands in a long line of labour controversies dating back to an animators’ strike in 1941, through protests about working conditions in the factories that produce Disney products, and most recently a series of layoffs across the company earlier this year.

There is a sense of something shared, however briefly and however manufactured, that I don’t find in many other places

Disney also has a decidedly mixed record on cultural issues. Writing in The Guardian in 2021, the journalist Steve Rose noted that:

Disney’s history of racist caricatures and ethnic stereotyping has been well documented and routinely criticised: the crows in Dumbo that drew on racist minstrel caricatures of African Americans; the Islamophobic tropes in Aladdin; the mockery of Native Americans in Peter Pan… the list goes on.

Meta has indefinitely delayed its proposed commercial terms of service, which would have permitted the company to scrape the websites of Meta Business account users.

On Thursday, the company took down the preview link to the proposed terms and published an update to its Business Help Center that reads: “We recently shared that we were updating the Meta Commercial Terms, Product Catalog Terms, Self-Serve Ad Terms, and Ad Creative Generative AI Terms. These updates are now paused and will not take effect on November 20, 2026. We are continuing to consult with stakeholders and will provide a further update when we have more to share. In the meantime, our existing terms remain in effect.”

Meta confirmed the indefinite delay in a statement to Nieman Lab. “We’re pausing the changes as we continue to engage with stakeholders and take our time to get this right,” said a spokesperson for the company.

Meta — which owns Facebook, Messenger, Instagram, WhatsApp, and Threads — has repeatedly pushed back the terms’ effective date since Nieman Lab first reported on them on October 15. The terms were first set to take effect on October 30, sparking global outcry among news publishers, politicians, and trade organizations. On October 16, Meta removed the word “train” from its terms and limited the use of future scraped content to “advertising and business products.” On October 23, Meta moved the effective date back by three weeks to November 20.

Last week, Meta pledged to consult news publishers and industry leaders ahead of putting new commercial terms into effect.

“We’ve heard publishers’ feedback on our proposed ads and business terms update. We care deeply about our partners and do not plan to make policy changes without a full consultation with industry groups and leaders,” vice president of communications Andy Stone tweeted on October 28. “We’re committed to getting this right, and as we expect this consultation could extend beyond November 20, in which case we’d delay implementation of the updated terms.”

Since then, courts in Norway and Brazil have issued preliminary injunctions to block the terms from taking effect as a result of lawsuits filed by media organizations in both countries. The United Kingdom’s Competition and Markets Authority has opened a formal investigation into Meta, examining whether the company was “abusing a dominant position by imposing exploitative terms on publishers and advertisers.”

In the United States, the proposed terms stoked bipartisan concern. At the end of October, Sens. Adam Schiff (D-Calif.) and Marsha Blackburn (R-Tenn.) sent letters to Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg asking him to withdraw the terms.

For Nikita Redkar, a big part of filming a video is putting together an outfit.

In a July video about youth-led protests in India, the 33-year-old is walking around New York City explaining how movements grow when people with opposing views come together on the things they do agree on. She’s wearing a white tube top and black jeans with sunglasses holding her hair back, along with a matching gold necklace and earrings that look like soda can tabs. You can’t see her shoes, but they clack enough for you to know she’s wearing a heel.

In another about comedian Shane Gillis’s Saturday Night Live monologue in which he called women “whores” for wearing shorts to the gym, she’s seated on the floor of her living room wearing a black silk velvet top with a pink faux-fur collar and sleeve cuffs. In the style of a Get Ready With Me video, she explains how 2000s comedy and pop culture entrenched misogynistic ideas of gender roles while applying her makeup.

A full-time news creator who mostly focuses on American politics and culture through a leftist and feminist lens, Redkar calls herself a “professor at Bimbo University.” The girliness is the point, she told me.

“I want to show that you don’t have to sacrifice these parts of yourself to be taken seriously,” Redkar said. “You should be taken seriously no matter what.”

Four years into news content creation, Redkar has more than 943,000 TikTok followers, 674,000 Instagram followers, 33,000 YouTube subscribers, and 16,000 Substack subscribers. (Her handle on all of them is @nikitadumptruck.) She aims to explain issues in a way that’s funny and accessible — whether she’s attending protests outside the United Nations (“Get ready with me to bully Netanyahu”), traveling through Europe (“Spend the day in socialist hellhole Denmark with me”), or explaining the negative impacts of private equity companies (“A private equity boyfriend is this summer’s hottest accessory”).

Redkar and I chatted in October about how she does her job, leaning into her femininity to explain the news, and what her relationship with social media is like. Our conversation has been edited for length and clarity.

In 2022, I had a video that really took off — like millions of views within a few hours. I was explaining the Russian invasion of Ukraine with a silly metaphor about Russia being a jealous ex that doesn’t want to see his ex thrive and be independent.

I tried that formula again a couple weeks later…about NATO and fears of World War III. I explained exactly what would be affected. I said there’s not going to be a world war, but things are going to get really expensive, which happened. I also used a girly friendship metaphor for that video. That’s when I started doing that formula — leaning into hyper-femininity to explain these complex geopolitical topics.

It’s important to make information accessible because we are going through so much news-wise and not all of it is easy to understand. I enjoy bringing this information I’m naturally interested in to people in a way where everyone [can] get involved.

When I was starting, I was not [a stereotypical] history buff or a news junkie. I would like to think that someone who looks like me and talks like me should be just as interested in politics and just as interested in the outcome of this country.

It was really important to me to bring, colloquially speaking, the girls and the gays and the theys into the space, because it is fascinating and it provides context to what we’re going through right now. It makes the present a little less daunting when you study historical cycles and realize that people 100 years ago dealt with [similar things to what we’re going through now]. How did they come out of that?

I feel like leftist content creators all operate on a spectrum. You have people who are getting really deep into Marxist theory, for example, and things like geopolitics. I’m at the beginning. I’m the person who’s holding the door open and being like, “OK, you just got here, this is what we’re talking about right now.”

She was upset that I called my page Bimbo University. She was like, “You’re dumbing yourself down. Women shouldn’t dumb themselves down. You are just as smart as a man, if not smarter than a man.”

That was my lightbulb moment of, oh, your feminism has always been to measure your worth as equal to a man and by the standards of men…working toward a man’s acceptance. In some industries, you’ve got to do that. I don’t blame [people] for thinking like that.

You should be taken seriously no matter what.

My week is [split] between videos [on topics] that the general public is talking about, and videos that are just interesting to me. That’s how I stay sane in this business. A few months ago, an American friend of my spouse asked him to ask me: "Why is everyone suddenly saying alongside?" I hadn't noticed it at that point, but once he'd mentioned it, I felt surrounded by alongside.

As this Google Books ngram shows, the word has taken off in the 21st century:

Separating out the British and American books, we can see that this is a British-led trend.

Alongside climbed in British usage throughout the 20th century. American English suddenly decided to (orig. AmE) play catch-up in the 21st century.

This trend is observable in other corpora too. The News on the Web corpus, for example, shows more than double the rate of alongside in British news sources versus American ones.

And within the US News data, the rise of alongside has sped up since 2020.

Among(st) the prepositions, alongside is a relative (orig. AmE) newbie. In the OED, where it's marked as "originally nautical," its first citation is from 1704; its definition: "In a position parallel to; side by side with; close to the side of; next to, beside." So the examples are about boats positioned next to other boats or docks, etc. It seems to have gradually moved onto land, especially in the UK, in the 19th century.

So why have Americans suddenly (orig. AmE) taken a shine to alongside? Why is it more attractive than along or beside or next to? Wondering whether there was a trend toward(s) longer, British prepositions, I tried comparing it to amongst. But the more-BrE amongst seems to have peaked in AmE about 12 years ago:

In 2013, the online magazine Slate published an article by Ben Yagoda about Americans saying amongst instead of among. Perhaps once people were talking about the "British invasion" of amongst, Americans became more self-conscious about it. If Ben published an article about alongside, could that change its fortunes?

Having had alongside pointed out to me, I'm now self-conscious about using it. But this blog gives us a record of me using it:

- "BrE has kerb for the edging alongside a road" (curb/kerb, May 2020)

- "British pigs in blankets are small sausages wrapped in bacon (and cooked!). They are delicious. They're traditionally served alongside turkey as part of Christmas dinner." (pigs in blankets, Feb 2020)

- "I've seen a lot of "down with grammar!" messages, often alongside 'learning should be fun!'" (grammar is not the enemy, May 2016)

So, what do you think: do I sound Britified when I say such things, or is alongside completely international now?

***

PS: Searching for commentary about alongside, I found some concern about the use of alongside with. Further (orig. BrE) rooting around in the corpora, though, show that alongside with is a tiny proportion of alongside usages (0.7 per million words in AmE, 0.8 per million words in BrE in the NOW corpus).

item.description:

Why it is here: original reporting, evidence and concrete detail

The people at WordUnscrambler.pro sent me a list of "the most misspelled (BrE misspelt*) words" for the UK.

But I first have to gripe a bit. Here's the methodology:

We analyzed Jan 1, 2025 - Dec 17, 2025 search data from Google Trends for "How do you spell" and "How to spell".

That's not a method for discovering the "most misspelled words." That's a method for discovering the most looked-up spellings. This is the kind of (BrE) jiggery-pokery makes me hate headlines. If you think to look up a word, then you might be insecure or curious about its spelling. But that's keeping you from misspelling it. I'm betting that when they're not looking up spellings like these, those people are out in the world (like the rest of us) are confidently spelling accommodation with one m and letting spellcheck catch it for them (or not).

Nevertheless, the WU.pro folks showed admirable linguistic sensitivity in not declaring the Americanisms on the list "misspelled." Instead, they note repeatedly that both the US and UK variants "are correct".

United Kingdom's most misspelled words queried spellings:

1. Colour - 109 200 searches - Both colour and color are correct.

2. Favourite - 82 900 searches - Both favourite and favorite are correct.

3. License - 59 000 searches.

4. Diarrhoea - 58 700 searches - Both diarrhoea and diarrhea are correct.

5. Jewellery - 56 400 searches.

6. Definitely - 53 000 searches.

7. Auntie - 50 400 searches - Both auntie and aunty are correct.

8. Weird - 48 000 searches.

9. Business - 46 800 searches.

10. Behaviour - 40 800 searches - Both behaviour and behavior are correct.

11. Neighbour - 39 600 searches - Both neighbour and neighbor are correct.

12. Country - 29 000 searches.

13. Queue - 22 800 searches.

14. Gorgeous - 22 600 searches.

15. Necessary - 23 000 searches.

I've added the blue to show which ones are also on the US top 10, which I've copied at the bottom of this post.† (Not sure why the UK got a top 15 and the US a top 10. Nor why necessary has more searches but is lower on the list than queue.)

Some of these are definitely difficult—others, like country, surprised me. But let's have a little look at whether people do misspell them, using the Corpus of Global Web-Based English. (I'm using that one even though it's 13 years old now because web-based English is more likely to include misspellings than the published writing in other comparative corpora.) I won't try to cover all of them, just the ones that strike me as transatlantically interesting.

Postscript : On the same day as I wrote this post, another company released its (much better) analysis of British misspellings. See the bottom of this post for more on that.

US/UK variants

-or/-our

In that vein, the following graph shows that there's probably more AmE writing on UK websites than BrE writing on AmE websites—which is not so surprising, since there are presumably about 5 times more US than UK writers on the internet and text from American wire services and other companies might be reprinted wholesale on UK sites.

But the other thing to take from the our/or chart is: Canadian spelling is in crisis. The (standard Canadian) -our spellings only just outnumber the -or ones. Meanwhile, the Canadian Prime Minister recently got into trouble for using British -ise spellings that are not traditionally Canadian.

licence/license

License is a tricky one because it's the correct spelling for BrE, when it is a verb. But it is licence in BrE when it is a noun (s in AmE for both). The first chart here shows a lot of (incorrect for BrE) license as a noun in the GB corpus—but that will, again, be partly due to American writing on British websites, rather than British writers misspelling it. It's hard to know how much each factor contributes.

I was surprised not to see practice/practise on the UK misspelling list. You can read more about that at an older post, if you'd like to.

Diarrhea/diarrhoea

This one seems to have little to do with US/UK confusion. Diarrh(o)ea is just difficult and unpleasant for everyone. And personal: everybody's misspelling it their own ways:

(The crossed-out ones are names that happened to be caught on my search for "diarr*a". I don't envy them their diarr-a names.)

jewellery/jewelry

The later jewellery spelling seems to have derived from jeweller + y ('the stuff that the jeweller makes'—analogous to pottery) while jewelry derives from jewel+ry ('products created from jewels'—analogous to pastry, balladry). In 1901, the OED commented (about BrE usage):

In commercial use commonly spelt jewellery; the form jewelry is more rhetorical and poetic, and unassociated with the jeweller. But the pronunciation with three syllables is usual even with the former spelling.

So, we might consider jewelry to be AmE and old-fashioned BrE.

It's been my perception that weird is more a problem in UK spelling, and GloWbE bears that out a little bit, with wierd a greater proportion of the UK forms (about 3%) than the US (about 2%):

country

queue

The word is much more common in BrE, but hard to spell everywhere. And yet, people seem to mostly get it right. Leaving off the final e sometimes happens, but really not much:

I'd expected to find the word spelled like its homonyms cue and Q, but there aren't many such misspellings. For the following chart, I searched for queue, queu, que, Q and cue, but none of the queu spellings showed up in the 'in a' phrasing:

The Q spelling might be an abbreviation, rather than a misspelling. But it's striking that the cue homonym is absent from the British entirely. These people know a queue's a queue.

A 'wow' player - why Ngumoha is already a Liverpool game-changer

Rio Ngumoha is going to be a 'wow' player for Liverpool - and he showed everyone exactly what he is already capable of in Sunday's 4-0 win over Manchester United.

He made an outstanding assist then added a fine finish, and there is much more to come. He plays without fear so he is going to score and make many more goals the same way.

Ngumoha has only just turned 18 but he is already a game-changer, someone who gets people excited because he is so hard to stop when he is one-on-one.

Of course he can frustrate you at times too, but that's what creative and explosive wingers like him do - and it's because he is so talented that everyone wants to see an end product from him every time he gets on the ball.

There were times against United when Ngumoha did not quite deliver, but he is still so young and I would much rather see players like him take too many touches - or try too many things and fail - than be afraid to try them in the first place.

So, if he runs out of play or runs into too many players at times, because teams are doubling up on him like United were, that just shows how scared they are of him.

His ability means he occupies opposition players - Youri Tielemans was always backing up Diogo Dalot on his wing to try to help him out, but that just meant United were leaving someone else free.

Sometimes it is actually harder when you are playing out wide against 10 men because you don't get the same amount of space - United were not attacking the same way they would have done with 11, and they were sitting in more.

Yes, Ngumoha ran up the odd blind alley or got outnumbered but that is always going to happen. As he learns, and gets even better, his decision-making will improve too. He will know when to try to go past people or when to find that free man instead.

But he still showed all the bravery you want from a winger against United and, when you keep trying things the way he did, something is going to come off for you.

I look at Bradley Barcola in a similar way to Ngumoha - he can be frustrating but he tries things, and can be brilliant.

For Liverpool right now, one of the biggest positives is the competition they have in wide areas, with those two plus Victor Munoz and Cody Gakpo.

Two goals inside seven minutes from Tajon Buchanan and Tani Oluwaseyi gave Villarreal a commanding lead at Camp Nou and things got worse for Barça when winger Lamine Yamal missed a first-half penalty.

The Catalan giants fought back in style, striking three times in an 11-minute second-half spell to claim victory. Gerard Martín and Fermín López pulled Barça level before Pau Navarro’s own goal gave them victory.

Barça have now won four consecutive matches across all competitions since their Clàsico defeat by Real Madrid in October, and restored their three-point cushion over José Mourinho’s side, who had moved level with Saturday’s victory over Celta Vigo.

Buchanan fired Villarreal ahead in the fifth minute, producing a perfect sliced effort from distance after López gave the ball away. Two minutes later, the visitors doubled their lead through another Canadian, as Oluwaseyi broke down the left flank and smashed an effort into the roof of the net.

Gerwyn Price finally ended his major trophy drought by winning the Grand Slam of Darts and is delighted to silence his critics. The Welshman had not won a major televised event since 2022 and may have thought it might not happen again after losing three finals this year alone.

But with Luke Littler and Luke Humphries exiting early, Price took his chance with a brilliant 16-11 win over Gian van Veen in Wolverhampton. Price claimed Grand Slam glory for the fourth time, but this one will surely mean the most to him.

The 41-year-old, who swatted away a wasp and Kevin Doets in the semi-finals earlier on Sunday, was embroiled in a tense and nervy encounter which turned in the 15th leg. Van Veen had six darts to break for an 8-7 lead, but could not finish and Price seized the moment. Why it is here: In-depth analysis, nuanced discussion, and clear reporting on a significant educational issue.

The inspection and rating of schools is, by definition, a fraught process. There are few things that parents care more about than the education of their children. For teachers and headteachers, it is stressful and exposing to have their work judged. At a time when shrinking school rolls are leading to closures, the stakes are even higher. An unpopular school with empty places is far more likely to be asked to merge, or close, than one that is sought after by parents.

Policymakers have a tough job to strike a balance between the undeniable pressure that the watchdog places on schools in England and the benefits to families of information to aid their choices. But the coroner’s verdict on the death of Ruth Perry, a headteacher who took her own life in 2023, tipped the balance away from a system that relied too heavily on one-word judgments. The inspection that led to the downgrading of her primary school to “inadequate” was judged to have contributed to her death. In its 2024 manifesto, Labour promised to replace one-word labels with more nuanced overviews of schools’ performance.

But 12 months after the introduction of a report card to replace the old grades, Ofsted’s critics remain frustrated. The National Association of Head Teachers tried to challenge the revised framework in the high court. Two-thirds of teachers who responded to a survey said that the new inspections were as bad or worse than the old ones. In October the education secretary, Lucy Powell, said that further reforms were on the way. (After devolution in 1999, Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland rejected England’s model of school competition, academies and league tables.)

If, as expected, the framework is adjusted to take more account of a school’s context, and to ease workload pressures, that will be a good result. Analysis shows that schools in England with more deprived intakes are much less likely than schools with low deprivation to meet expected standards. This raises questions about whether inspections fairly account for the challenges facing schools in poorer areas. As well as being wrong in principle, a framework skewed against demanding socioeconomic conditions has practical effects, lowering morale in schools that are judged to be underachieving, and potentially making it harder for them to recruit staff.

The Department for Education and Ofsted must take responsibility for such missteps, and for an inspection regime that many now find more onerous. Advocates of more radical reforms, whose goal is a less adversarial alternative to Ofsted, should be listened to as part of this process. Peer review between schools can be a constructive route to improvement. Local authorities already monitor standards in the schools they oversee, as do academy trusts – although their highly uneven results offer some of the best evidence of the need for an independent inspectorate with a focus on governance as well as other aspects. Resource pressures must also be considered; the current level of funding does not enable the kind of exchange between inspectors and schools that some would like.

It is shocking and tragic that Ofsted needed a coroner’s warning to seemingly recognise its duty to treat school staff with courtesy and respect. The new framework, evidence suggests, remains flawed. Ms Powell must ensure that inspections help schools improve, rather than merely find fault.

The Providence School Board approved a nearly $200,000 separation package for outgoing Providence Public School District Superintendent Javier Montañez at its Wednesday night meeting.

November 10, 2026

Oleksiy Honcharuk

In late 2023, Ukraine’s military leadership faced an institutional choice: establish a dedicated branch of the armed forces for unmanned systems or integrate drones into existing branches. Most senior officers I knew opposed the separate force, and their strongest argument was sound within classical doctrine. Each branch of service corresponds to a distinct domain of war: The army fights on land, the navy at sea, the air force in the air. Unmanned systems operate across all of these domains and possess none of their own. No domain, no branch of service. The advocates were mostly newcomers from civilian life, and the opponents were career generals. Within the coordinate system of existing doctrine, the generals were right. The war itself, however, was about to overtake their premise that it unfolds in fixed places. Ukraine created the Unmanned Systems Forces anyway, the first branch of its kind in the world. A force with about 2.5 percent of Ukraine’s military personnel has accounted for roughly a third of Russian losses this past year.

That decision reflected a collision of two cultures. People who entered from civilian life built a different culture: continuous experimentation in place of pre-defined standards and protocols, openness to mistakes as the price of learning, and the habit of improving weapons in combat. For career officers, the question was usually one of means: which systems, in what quantity, and for which branch. The real question lies elsewhere: What game are we playing, and how do we imagine it?

The decisive dimension of the war in Ukraine is not where forces fight, but how fast each side adapts. A unit that updates its tactics and technology every six weeks does not cancel the firepower of a unit that updates once a year — a slower side can still pay in mass, as Russia does. What the faster unit wins is time: It sets the terms of every exchange for as long as the gap lasts. Mass decides how long a side can continue to pay, and speed determines how much each payment buys. I call this the Time Domain: a competition not for territory but for time itself — the interval between the moment a new capability reaches the front and the point at which the enemy’s answer to it works — won by whoever adapts faster. It is also an answer to the generals: The Unmanned Systems Forces do have a battleground of their own — not a place on the map, but a contest, the one their machines are built to win faster than anyone else.

When Russia launched its full-scale invasion, I returned to Ukraine from Stanford to help its fight. I worked inside Aerorozvidka, the volunteer community that pioneered network-centric warfare in Ukraine and helped create the Delta battlefield management system around a single conviction: push battlefield information outward, to those who act on it, instead of holding it inside headquarters. Later, I advised the first commander of the Unmanned Systems Forces and built the team that created the 412th Brigade “Nemesis.”

Throughout this war, Russia has held superiority across every parameter a classical analyst would measure: personnel, artillery, missiles, armor. Under that asymmetry, innovation speed was never an advantage for Ukraine. It was a condition of existence.

The best commanders I worked with understood this intuitively: Tactics had to change faster, commanders had to build units differently, and time was the decisive resource. But they had no language to explain it to headquarters, no metric for a manufacturer, no concept to make it a requirement for doctrine. The analytical apparatus of military thought describes who stands where and how much each side has. It has no category for how quickly a force is becoming something else.

Military doctrine treats a domain as the environment in which operations take place, and NATO recognizes five: land, sea, air, cyberspace, and space. Each answers the question of “where.” But consider an ordinary grass field. People can play football, field hockey, and rugby on the same ground. The ground is identical, yet each game has its own team, its own rules, its own way of winning. The field does not define the game — the rules do. The pattern holds here, too: a distinct game with its own objective and rules, one a force wins on its own terms. Cyberspace earned its spot on the list not because it occupies a physical location, but because the contest there follows a logic the older categories never captured. This is what happened with Ukraine’s drone units. On that shared field, they were playing by rules nobody had written down, and they created a new game: a technology race detached from any portion of space, yet decisive in what happens on the ground. That is the game Ukraine built the Unmanned Systems Forces to play. “I wanted disciplined but not regimented thinking. Commanders must encourage intellectual risk-taking to preclude a lethargic environment. Leaders must shelter those challenging nonconformists and mavericks who make institutions uncomfortable; otherwise you wash out innovation.”

— James Mattis & Bing West, Call Sign Chaos

For the last decade, the Pentagon has had the authorities to buy commercially derived technologies at speed and scale, but not enough people who know how to use those authorities. Successive senior Pentagon leaders, both military and civilian, have asserted that these technologies will prove decisive in future wars. Panels, commissions, and directives created new pathways and the Pentagon’s Acquisition Transformation Strategy now makes commercial-first buying a top priority.

This article argues that the Defense Innovation Unit should lead the implementation of this transformation by becoming the department’s weapons school for commercial technology acquisition. Like the Navy and Air Force weapons schools, the unit should select promising servicemembers, train them rigorously, credential them visibly, and ultimately send them back to the services to lead and teach others. Two things make this work: training that turns motivated people into experts and incentives that ensure that time at the unit enhances their careers instead of ending them. The mavericks that built the unit had the first without the second, and many paid for it dearly.

Since 2016, the Defense Innovation Unit has executed hundreds of commercial solutions openings using other transaction agreements through partnerships with limited groups of service personnel whose acquisition knowledge has never scaled. The unit’s experience will be the bedrock of the curriculum.

In November 2014, then-Secretary of Defense Chuck Hagel announced that the Department of Defense was implementing a Third Offset Strategy in response to renewed Russian aggression in Eastern Europe and China’s militarization of the South China Sea. The strategy would “start with a clean sheet of paper” to field several commercially derived technologies, including robotics and autonomous systems. As a part of this strategy, Hagel’s successor, Secretary of Defense Ash Carter, announced that the Pentagon would be establishing a storefront in Silicon Valley called the Defense Innovation Unit Experimental.

In 2016, the unit’s three-person acquisition pathways team constructed a competitive solicitation process called a commercial solutions opening: a-three phase competition emphasizing speed, flexibility, and collaboration in the contracting process by using other transaction agreements, which played a prodigious role in winning the space race and had been re-invigorated by the 2016 National Defense Authorization Act. Using this process made the Pentagon a more appealing customer and leveled the playing field for startups by driving a commercial-friendly approach that recognized startups and their investors’ expectations by providing buy signals at the speed of business, not typical defense acquisition cycles.

From 2016 to 2024, the unit remained separated and secluded from the rest of the Pentagon. The unit had a modest budget, relying on motivated mission partners to fund projects. Servicemembers at the unit were mavericks whose intrinsic motivation to make an impact took precedence over promotion and advancement. They repeatedly warned the rest of the Pentagon about the threat of small drones to parked aircraft, the outsized role of drones in the Nagorno-Karabakh War, and the rapid proliferation of high-quality commercial satellite imagery. Despite complete alignment with the Third Offset Strategy, their warnings were routinely dismissed. While the unit punched well above its weight, it suffered budget cuts and spurious contract award protests. In 2021, Director Mike Brown was nominated to be the Pentagon’s top acquisitions official, only to have his nomination derailed by unsubstantiated accusations of abusing hiring authorities. These events led many at the unit to perceive themselves as rebels resisting bloated Pentagon bureaucracy. Many servicemembers were shuffled back to the services where their careers were negatively impacted. One of us served as the unit’s first warfighter-in-residence, arriving ecstatic at the opportunity to make an impact on capabilities for his community. While many projects worked on were successful, it also meant permanently derailing the author’s military career.

Some of the unit’s most successful projects, including Persistent Maritime Intelligence, Surveillance, and Reconnaissance, Construction Scale Additive Manufacturing, and Peacetime Indications and Warning, came from coincidental alignment between funded mission problems and solutions from vendors like SailDrone, ICON Technology, Capella Space, and others whose founders hadn’t imagined the military as a customer.

Reform and the Conservatives under Kemi Badenoch, both of whom welcomed Trump’s re-election in 2024, have increasingly tried to dissociate themselves from the US president amid questions over his temperament and judgment, while his attacks on Iran have driven up global energy prices.

Why it is here: Discussion of political trends with useful vocabulary and context.

Data centers were on the ballot, both directly and indirectly, in the 2026 midterm elections.

A total of 41 local ballot initiatives concerning data centers in 10 states were up for a vote. All but one resulted in measures to restrict or limit their development.

The centers also may have played a role in several high-profile contests. In Ohio’s race for a U.S. Senate seat, Democratic challenger Sherrod Brown hammered incumbent Jon Husted for his past support of data centers. In Texas, Gina Hinojosa made Republican Gov. Greg Abbott’s track record of supporting tax breaks for data centers a focal point of her winning campaign. Her victory marked a historic break with decades of Republican control in the state. As governor-elect, she immediately reaffirmed her campaign pledge to pursue legislation protecting Texans from data centers.

According to NBC exit poll data, 56% of voters felt that data centers were a major or even a crucial factor in influencing their congressional vote. For Black voters, the share was even higher, at 68%.

Data centers are key components in artificial intelligence infrastructure, housing the computing resources used to train AI models. These massive facilities guzzle energy and water and are very noisy. Many Americans argue that their costs, in terms of land use, higher utility bills and environmental degradation, outweigh the benefits.

I’m a professor of political science who studies political parties, electoral politics and technology. My forthcoming book, “Democratic Intelligence: Navigating Electoral Politics in an AI World,” examines how the adoption of this technology is reshaping established practices and power dynamics in campaigns.

Before the midterms, it had already appeared to be disrupting some partisan alignments. Following those historic elections, which have thoroughly shaken up America’s political geography, the widespread pushback against data centers is now part of the narrative explaining the dramatic results of the 2026 midterms.

Disrupting political polarization

In contrast to many other issues, concern about data centers is relatively bipartisan. The Annenberg Public Policy Center asked Americans in mid-2026 whether they support or oppose having data centers in their communities. Opposition was stronger among Democrats, at 69%, than Republicans, at 54%, but it crossed party lines.

Local ballot measures restricting data centers also cut across traditional political alignments. Communities as disparate as deeply red Edgewater, Florida, and solidly blue Alhambra, California, voted to prohibit them. The margins for the restrictions were large, averaging 49 percentage points.

The one restrictive local measure that failed to pass was in Harwood, North Dakota, population around 800. With a data center project already in progress, political and economic leaders prevailed in arguing that restrictions would cut into local revenue and stifle economic development more generally.

Allies and adversaries

Exit polls taken during the midterm elections also detected a degree of bipartisanship. Of the 56% of voters who said data centers played a “major” or “crucial” role in their vote, approximately two-thirds were Democrats and one-third Republicans. Exit polls, however, should be interpreted with care, given their methodological limitations.

These responses hint at why the narrative that opposition to data centers helped fuel the Democrats’ historic midterm victory emerged right away.

The seeds of this argument were in place before the election, picking up on unusual alliances that marked the data center opposition. In cities and counties, zoning fights are drawing a diverse kind of resistance: environmentalists, voters reeling under high electricity costs, local-control advocates and farmers concerned that data centers eat up land. They unite in opposition to projects backed by powerful corporate interests.

Some of the bipartisanship around this issue has even seeped into Congress. Several weeks before Election Day, the House passed the Ratepayer Protection Act by a 417-3 vote. The bill would require states to consider adopting a policy that data centers pay for the upgrades necessary to meet their high electricity needs. The three nay House votes were from progressives who felt the bill’s measures, which would be voluntary, didn’t go far enough to protect consumers.

Similar concerns killed the Senate version, a reminder that even allies sometimes follow different strategic paths. Some proponents of tighter regulation will accept incremental progress, while others push for more sweeping change.

Brookings Institution scholars anticipate that the newly elected Congress will take up the issue again, this time with a directive to states to establish mandatory, not voluntary, requirements.

Politics as usual

As the midterm elections approached, candidates up and down the ballot blanketed the airwaves and digital platforms with ads against data centers. President Donald Trump pushed back, suggesting that data center opponents want their communities to be “backwards and poor.”

Some Republican candidates walked a fine line between responding to voters’ concerns and not alienating the president.

It matters little whether the data center electoral narrative is accurate, and so far, the reported evidence is limited. We need to know where losing candidates stood on data centers, not just the winners. That voters considered data centers important says nothing about which direction they leaned. And despite a 98% success rate across the 41 local ballot measures, it’s hard to gauge how much resistance there is to the more than 600 proposed data centers that are slated to be built.…

This section details how Pew Research Center used data on age, fertility, mortality, migration and religious switching from 201 countries and territories around the world to make estimates of global religious populations in 2020, and to project how those populations will change in the years up to and including 2070.

It uses a question-and-answer format to go through the methods used by Center researchers in the Future of World Religions report.

Q1: How did Pew Research Center estimate baseline figures for 2020?

Q2: How does Pew Research Center’s projection model work?

Q3: How do the results in this study compare with prior Pew Research Center studies?

- The 2015 “Future of World Religions” projections

- The 2017 “Europe’s Growing Muslim Population” projections

- The 2022 “Modeling the Future of Religion in America” projections

Q4: How do you define regions, countries and territories?

This work was a collaboration between researchers at Pew Research Center and the Center for Advanced Studies of Population and Religion (CASPAR) at Krakow University of Economics.

Q1: How did Pew Research Center estimate baseline figures for 2020?

The starting point of a population projection is called a baseline, and in this study the baseline is the year 2020. The demographic methods we used to project populations of religious groups required collecting and standardizing massive amounts of input data about these groups (in each country and territory) for the baseline year, including each group’s population size as well as its age and sex composition. We also needed data for each group (in each country and territory) on patterns of fertility, mortality, migration and religious switching.

The next sections describe how we measured these baseline characteristics.

Estimating religious composition

Using census and survey data information about religious identities, we sorted the global population into seven religious groups: Christians, Muslims, Hindus, Buddhists, Jews, followers of other religions and religiously unaffiliated people. The “other religions” category includes Baha’is, Daoists (also spelled Taoists), Jains, Shintoists, Sikhs, Wiccans, Zoroastrians and many small groups, some of which can be described as folk or traditional religions. The religiously unaffiliated population – sometimes called “nones” – includes people who in surveys and censuses answer a religious affiliation question by saying they do not identify with any religion or that they are atheist or agnostic.

Most of the census and survey data came from questions that measure religion using a direct question like “What is your religion, if any?” The census and survey questions either ask this question by itself, or, less often, they first ask a filter question such as “Do you belong to a religion or religious denomination?”94

It’s worth noting that we rely on how people describe their own religious identity, regardless of whether that identity lines up perfectly with belief or practice. When someone identifies with a particular religious group, we classify them as being part of that group regardless of their beliefs and practices. For example, if someone identifies as Christian, we classify them as Christian whether or not they hold Christian beliefs that may be considered orthodox or attend worship services. Similarly, if someone identifies with no religion, we classify them as religiously unaffiliated even if they hold at least some religious beliefs and attend worship services.

The censuses and surveys we use classify the religious identity of respondents at varying levels of specificity. For example, depending on the source, the most specific level of affiliation measured for a Southern Baptist could be Christian, Protestant, Baptist or Southern Baptist. Researchers coded all religious identities into one of the seven categories used in this study.

Sources used to measure religious composition

The baseline estimates of the 2020 religious population, which we used as the starting point for our projections through 2070, were first published in Pew Research Center’s 2025 report “How the Global Religious Landscape Changed from 2010 to 2020.” That report was based on more than 2,700 data sources, including censuses; large-scale demographic surveys (which often survey more than 10,000 people); general population surveys (which typically survey 1,000 to 3,000 people); information from population registers; the World Religion Database; and government reports.

The vast majority of data underlying the 2020 baseline estimates came from four main types of primary sources: general population surveys; censuses; large-scale demographic surveys; and the World Religion Database.

General population surveys were our primary source to measure the religious composition of an assortment of countries and territories that make up 44% of the world’s population.

Census data was our primary source in countries where 42% of the global population lives. We relied on large-scale demographic surveys, including Demographic and Health Surveys (DHS), as our primary sources for 10% of the world’s people in 2020.

Additionally, we used World Religion Database (WRD) estimates as our primary source in places that are home to 3% of the world’s people. Among the many types of information used to create WRD estimates are statistics gathered from religious communities and assessments from country experts. This type of information is especially valuable for countries like Cuba and North Korea, which have little or no nationally representative census or survey data on religious composition that is publicly available.…

item.title: Sounds may seem louder or even painful as you age. Here’s why
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Clear, well-structured explanation of a complex phenomenon with useful vocabulary.

Loud noises bother some people more as they get older – the clatter of plates or shrieking children, which once blended into the background, now seem utterly intolerable. If that’s you, it’s worth knowing what’s due to normal ageing and what isn’t.

What is sound hypersensitivity?

For some people, everyday sounds become hard to bear. Some researchers call this sound hypersensitivity, an umbrella term for several conditions.

There’s some disagreement about the names and definitions of these conditions, which makes it hard to determine how common they are. One of them is noise sensitivity, a tendency to feel annoyed or overwhelmed by ongoing background noise. Others include hyperacusis, in which ordinary sounds feel uncomfortably loud or even painful; misophonia, or intense anger, disgust or anxiety in response to specific sounds (For example: another person’s breathing); and phonophobia, the fear that a sound will cause discomfort.

What causes sound hypersensitivity?

Scientists don’t fully understand why everyday sounds become hard to tolerate for certain people. Daniel Polley, a neuroscientist who directs the Lauer Tinnitus Research Center at Mass Eye and Ear in Boston, suspects some of the discomfort is a natural response to an increasingly industrialized and noisy world full of sounds we can’t control.

“As we age, we get a bit more rigid about what it is that we want going into our bodies,” he says, “including sound waves”.

That said, researchers are investigating a range of possible explanations. They haven’t pinned down a brain change that explains any one type of sound hypersensitivity, but people at higher risk for certain types include those with hearing loss, tinnitus (chronic ringing or buzzing in the ears), and neuropsychiatric conditions like autism. Much of what’s known about possible mechanisms of sound hypersensitivity comes from rodent studies, so there are still big questions about what’s happening in people.

A leading theory is called central gain, which relates to hearing loss. According to this theory, when damage to the inner ear weakens the signal it sends to the brain, the brain turns up its own amplification to compensate. As a result, it perceives a small increase in volume as much larger, which makes sounds seem louder than they really are. “The perception of sound isn’t generated in the ear; it’s generated in the brain,” says Polley.

Possible triggers are changes to the inner ear caused by age, noise exposure, or both. These can result in the loss of cells that amplify sound, and fraying of the auditory nerve that carries those cells’ signals to the brain.

Some people with sound hypersensitivity have hearing loss they don’t know about. Routine testing may not clarify things either, because standard hearing tests don’t pick up auditory nerve damage. As a result, some people with this type of hearing loss may struggle to follow conversations in noisy places but pass a hearing test.

What can you do about sound hypersensitivity?

There’s no medication that reliably eliminates sound hypersensitivity or reverses inner ear damage. However, certain strategies can lower your risk and ease symptoms.

The most important preventive step is to protect your ears from loud noise. Long or repeated exposure to sounds at 85 decibels or more, like those from speaker-heavy concerts, lawnmowers and leaf blowers, can damage your hearing. Wearing ear protection can delay that damage, although some wear comes with age no matter what.

If you suspect you already have some sound hypersensitivity, noise-canceling earbuds can quickly cut loud background noise while still letting you hear sounds you choose, says Polley. Earplugs also work, but they block everything, including sounds you may need or want to hear.

Just be aware that overprotecting your hearing can backfire. Shutting out too much sound may prompt the brain to turn up its amplification even further, which can worsen sound hypersensitivity. In one small study, people with normal hearing who wore earplugs for two weeks became less tolerant of loud sounds. “Isolating yourself, like going monastic, is not necessarily the right approach,” says Polley.

In one trial, people who did cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) tolerated louder sounds. This type of talk therapy can help sufferers avoid sounds less, face uncomfortable sounds gradually and feel less threatened by them. Some kinds of sound hypersensitivity are closely tied to anxiety and depression, and it’s possible treating those conditions can reduce symptoms.

When should you see a clinician?

Get help if sound hypersensitivity is causing you a lot of anxiety, disrupting your sleep or getting in the way of daily life, says Polley. Audiologists are usually the first point of contact. They can test your hearing and refer you to other specialists if needed.

If sounds hurt your ears, you may require a more cautious treatment approach. See a clinician, who may order brain imaging to rule out a growth on the auditory nerve.

If you have tinnitus, mention it to your clinician, as it often comes with sound hypersensitivity. Also take note if only one ear is affected; this may point to a specific cause that needs attention.

Regarding Polly Hudson’s article (At 17, I dated a 36-year-old. That decision looks very different to me now, 15 November), I met and lived with a 35-year-old man when I was 17. It is obvious now that the relationship was coercively controlling. A divorced father, he had a need to control every aspect of my life, so no makeup, no northern accent, no fatty food (I became anorexic), no scent, no staying out, no heels, no clothes he didn’t like.

I learned that he had done it all before, pursuing schoolgirls. I tried to break free multiple times, only to find that he had phoned my new partner, or read my diary so he could block my plans. This is about having control, it is not just a sexual preference.

The men doing this are rarely satisfied, and criticism can escalate to coercive, emotionally abusive levels. In some cases (though not in mine) girls are pimped out, shared with the man’s friends, imprisoned against their will.

To girls impressed by confidence, older men initially seem a catch. As for the father-daughter dynamic, a psychologist needs to pick apart why a grown man wants a sexual partner whom he treats like a daughter. I was seeking the father’s unconditional love and guidance that I never had. We’ve all heard of “daddy issues” – why do some men have “daughter issues”?

Name and address supplied

Polly Hudson should not be angry with her younger self. Would she be angry with another young girl who found herself in similar circumstances? Unlikely. There is something else that has stopped us speaking out: fear. Fear of physical or verbal retaliation by the perpetrator; of the judgment of those around us; of a legal system that fails to punish abusers and shames victims with hackneyed tropes that have long been disproven; of public and private organisations that continue to bury abuse allegations and enable perpetrators who bring in cash, clicks, viewers or shareholders.

Nevertheless, the more we talk, the harder it is for them to get away with it. Things are painfully slowly changing.

Michelle Stiles

Falmouth, Cornwall

It may be wise to increase the age of consent to 18 and I believe that victims of abusive relationships or rape need much better support. But the implications that arise from Gaby Hinsliff’s article (Don’t wait for a change in sexual consent law. Adults can act to stop age-gap abuse, 17 November) made me extremely uncomfortable.

My first serious relationship was with a man aged 33 when I was 18. He was both loving and affectionate, but the way in which people were so judgmental of both of us, and the implication drawn by other people that he must have been a pervert, made the relationship impossible.

I am now in my 30s and will be marrying a man in his 50s next month. We know that some people judge us based purely on our ages. It has made me reluctant to even post photos online of us as a couple. The only time that I have been in a relationship with an abusive element, the man was just a year older than I was. But there was never any automatic negative assumption about my relationship with him by others.

I want all victims of abuse to be empowered to seek justice and be supported in doing so. But there is a serious danger that we will reinforce the worst negative stereotypes of age-gap relationships while at the same time creating a false belief that relationships between people of the same age, or just a few years difference, are somehow inherently less likely to involve abuse or manipulation.

Bristol

Sarah Blaffer Hrdy’s research offers an important challenge to one of our most persistent assumptions about masculinity: that nurturing is somehow contrary to male nature (Would more hands-on dads create a more peaceful world? This pioneering scientist thinks so, 17 November). As a clinical psychotherapist, I find the most compelling implication is not simply that children benefit from involved fathers, but that fathers themselves may change through the experience of caring.

We often imagine psychological development as a process in which attitudes must change before behaviour follows. Yet caregiving may work in both directions. Repeated experiences of responding to another person’s vulnerability can engage and potentially strengthen the biological and psychological systems involved in emotional responsiveness, attachment and cooperation.

But we should be cautious about extending this into the claim that more nurturing fathers would necessarily produce a more peaceful world. Human beings are capable of extraordinary tenderness towards their own children while remaining hostile towards those outside their immediate circle. Empathy can be selective, and the causes of collective violence extend far beyond individual temperament.

Perhaps the more important question is whether the emotional capacities developed through caregiving can be extended towards strangers, communities and people with whom we disagree.

The significance of Hrdy’s work is not that nurturing makes men less masculine. It is that nurturing was never incompatible with masculinity in the first place.

Gareth Strangemore-Jones

Founder, Mental Health Matrix

My knees aren’t in terribly good condition. I’m at that age.

A few years ago, I was at a big hippy festival out in the Australian desert near Deniliquin. There, I attended a talk and was sitting down on the ground at the rear of a large group of people listening to a speaker. When the talk finished, everybody got up to leave, streaming past me as they went.

My fragile knees make it difficult for me to get up off the ground, and I didn’t want to attempt the manoeuvre in a crowd of people churning around me. So I thought, well, I’ll just sit here until they’ve all walked past, and then I’ll get up.

It was a bit humiliating sitting there in a sea of legs and feet; dust kicking up around me. Embarrassed, I had my head down.

And then this hand just appeared in front of me. I understood the gesture, which was, “Do you want help getting up?” I took the hand and, as the person pulled me to my feet, I saw it was a beautiful young man in his 20s. Once I was on my feet, we just smiled at each other. He walked off to do whatever he was going to do next, and I did the same.

For a woman getting into the age bracket where young men, in particular, don’t see you – in fact, they often have the propensity to not just ignore you but actively be rude – it challenged all my notions of who to be wary of, and who I could count on. This young man took the time to notice the middle-aged woman sitting in the dust and didn’t just walk past. He reached out, with an offer of humanity so perfect and so genuine.

That stranger, decades my junior, taught me that it only takes a second to make someone feel seen, and that second can make all the difference to your day, or your experience of yourself. I hope he’s gone on to have a fabulous life.

item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Engaging article about a unique location with cultural context and vivid descriptions.

There’s a now-iconic line from The Simpsons, which aired more than 30 years ago, where Principal Skinner is trying to track down Bart, who has skipped school.

He goes looking for him in places he assumes children might hang out, including a museum and a youth group, but finds them empty.

He pauses and considers: “Am I so out of touch? … No. It’s the children who are wrong.”

I find myself asking a similar question perched on Ebenezer Place in Adelaide, recently ranked the world’s 19th coolest street by Time Out magazine.

Sipping on a glass of Gamay at 4pm on a Saturday at French brasserie Hey Jupiter, I look down the street to assess the level of “coolness” that convinced a global magazine this is one of the 28 streets in the world most worth visiting.

Adelaide is no stranger to the dizzying highs of global magazine lists, placing in the top 10 of the Economist’s most liveable cities index for eight of the past 10 years, much to the bemusement of the higher-ranked Melbourne and Sydney. But this time it has won out: the only other Australian entry on the Time Out list – Ward Avenue in Sydney’s Potts Point – is ranked No 24.

In coolness, Adelaide wins.

Hey Jupiter is softening me to this idea. The French brasserie, with its vibrant green facade, sits alongside a South African eatery, vintage clothing outlet, record store and a jeweller.

The tree-lined street is open to one-way traffic and cars circle looking for a prime parking spot. Yet despite this it’s clean, bright and well-manicured, much like the crowd of young fashionistas and well-dressed older couples soaking up the vibe and sipping everything from vibrant matcha to lethal-looking martinis.

Almost two decades ago, that would have been me.

While diligently avoiding my university lectures, I would waste days – and nights – at a clothing store owned by my two best mates, which opened here in the mid-2000s.

I certainly thought it was cool then.

Edgy fashion outlets attracted musical acts like Van She and Pnau, who would randomly arrive along the strip with drinks in hand from a nearby wine store, as music wafted out of the shopfronts.

With street parties and events sponsored by big tobacco, there was a time when this street was the wild west of Adelaide’s east end.

Twenty years later, Ebenezer Place has had a glow-up, got some new roommates and been officially recognised as cool.

Christopher Arblaster, co-founder of clothing store Shop Pond (formerly A Flat Shop), also runs the adjacent vintage store, Filter Store. While surprised by the nomination, he’ll happily take the hype.

“I think it shows more about the people who use the street. We have lovely neighbours, some really great shops and there’s quite a lot of activity along here for a quieter strip,” he says.

“I wouldn’t say it’s the 19th coolest street in the world – but it is a nice place to be.”

Surprise shout-out

It’s not that Ebenezer Place doesn’t deserve the accolade – but what, exactly, are the criteria?

Time Out recommends visitors to the street “keep the vibes high” at nearby drinking haunts Nola and East End Cellars, catch an indie film at Palace Nova, or dine at Michelin Guide-recognised restaurants Golden Boy and Africola.

It names Ebenezer Place as the destination but suggests you widen the net some 500m to visit other restaurants on the city’s edge. It also points readers towards Rundle Street for its indie boutiques and high-end fashion labels.

The City of Adelaide seems equal parts excited and caught off-guard about the shout-out, posting a gushing message to social media with a photo of the wrong East End strip – bustling Vardon Avenue, not Ebenezer Place.

As 21-year-old Nicolas Garcia-Bellido Rodriguez and his mate, 20-year-old Eamon Ziersch-O’Connor, enjoy an ice-cream at Ovo Coffee and Gelato, they say the strip evokes another continent entirely.

“It feels like I’m in Europe sitting here, and parts of Rundle Street feel the same too,” Nicolas says.

“I think it’s the proximity – it’s right near the Exeter hotel, which is great. It hosts a lot of events here, which I think contributes to the vibe.”

Ata Alrimawi, 22, says the strip is his go-to place to relax and grab a coffee.

“I wouldn’t say top 20 in the world, but it’s the best in Adelaide for sure,” he says.

The state MP and minister for Adelaide, Lucy Hood, says the global ranking speaks to the passion and dedication of local businesses that have transformed Ebenezer Place into “a thriving and must-visit destination”.

A subjective list will always attract clicks and is rarely without its controversies. As my Gamay reaches the end of its final pour and the afternoon slips into evening, the people-watching has provided hours of entertainment.

I would still argue the judges must have had a pretty biblical night along this street to convince them it’s one of the 20 best in the world.

But Ebenezer Place has always had its charms. As the sun fades, I decide to embrace this new, if surprising chapter in the story of this understated 120-metre long strip. Maybe it’s me who’s out of touch, and the children were right all along.

item.title: Readers reply: when does a reasonable train route become unreasonable?
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Clean-up failed for this item, so the body is a truncated excerpt of the original.)

Why it is here: Reader engagement piece with varied opinions, but lacks depth in analysis.

I recently made a return trip to Edinburgh from London on which both legs of the journey were either significantly delayed or cancelled. At Waverley station, a message over the public address system told us we could travel by any “reasonable” route, but what does that mean? What counts as reasonable and what doesn’t? And who decides? Grant, by email

Send new questions to nq@theguardian.com.

Readers reply

When does a reasonable train route become unreasonable? When it’s no longer on track. Sagarmatha1953

I’ll guess that an Edinburgh to London route that involves a two-week stopover in Paris will not be considered “reasonable”. DeclineToState

Surely just any route in a roughly straight line to where you are going? The only catch would be when you’ve bought a split ticket using specific companies. My daughter recently had a cancelled train travelling from Glasgow to Leeds, but because it was a split ticket via Carlisle, anything on the east coast line was out of the question. On the plus side, she’d paid a small amount extra for some insurance and got £50 back for a £20 ticket (student railcard, before anyone gets excited by the price). She also found that, contrary to my expectations, the staff in the information desk at Glasgow station were incredibly helpful, so that’s probably a good place to start. Esollec

Since flying tends to be cheaper than trains, on this journey it would in theory be reasonable, but I doubt they’d consider it so. Plus the cost to the environment may not be thought reasonable. LorLala

The public address system told us we could travel by any “reasonable” route, but what does that mean? I suspect when it comes to making a claim for a delayed or cancelled journey, it means you have a battle on your hands. salamandertome

It would be reasonable to go from Edinburgh to London via Glasgow. It would be unreasonable to go via Glasgow and Plymouth. thenewschmoo

Of course. But there are more nuanced journeys, aren’t there. These are extremes. But there is a line that will differentiate reasonable and unreasonable, and I guess the letter-writer wants to know how that is determined and by whom. lexicon_mistress

There’s a set of routing guides that covers most situations: for instance, if you want to go between London and Edinburgh you can go via Glasgow, via Sheffield, via Leeds, via Doncaster, etc. This is always allowed if you have an Any Permitted Route ticket. If you have a ticket which specifies an operator or a route, then it may be acceptable to take a different route. You’d need to check with staff. TheNewNo2

I don’t want to research train routes myself – I want an employee of the railway company to be on hand to advise me. This is why I always go by car, although Edinburgh to London is a bit of a stretch. Goldgreen

An actual person on hand to give actual advice? What a quaint concept these days … Kevcoe

There are rules, obviously. A direct train is always reasonable, however circuitous the route. As is a route up to three miles longer than the shortest possible route. Passing through the same station twice isn’t generally reasonable, apart from a specific list of “easements” where it makes sense to take a fast train that passes through your final destination shortly before stopping at major hub or terminus. You might think that any route that is faster than the shortest route is also reasonable, but this isn’t automatic. Strictly speaking, you need to check the manual, as other answers have said. During significant disruption (when it is announced that other companies are accepting tickets), staff apply their discretion, which was a bit of a lottery. Until last month, when we got the right to travel by any route suggested by the National Rail journey planner. MickeyFinn

An extra three miles doesn’t give options anywhere except major cities! zxcv11

It reads more like a chance or community chest card joke, so I’m not sure they are being serious. Luxembourgpro

Absolutely true, although I agree it sounds like parody. It’s called the Common Routing Point Rule. The National Routing Guide glossary (quoted below) is very clear on this point. MickeyFinn

When a journey is between stations that have one or more common routeing points, the permitted journey takes the route of shortest distance or any route no more than 3 miles longer, whether or not they pass through the common routeing point. Also permitted are journeys that use direct trains to and from the common routeing point.

A reasonable train route becomes unreasonable when the fare is too high. I always check for split-ticketing options and go the long way round if it’s cheaper, and not too much further. Much more reasonable! Rattandy

I reckon you’d have a reasonable case as long as you’re heading in the right general direction. Grumpyoldgit999

I’d say the quickest alternative route by train, assuming at least five minutes leeway each time you change trains, is the reasonable route. Anything other than that and they could argue that your ticket isn’t valid. That’s if they check the ticket – which they often don’t, particularly when staff are having to deal with disruption. RobertMeyerFunnell

The question-setter almost certainly has a ticket issued by a specific train company – LNER for the east coast mainline or Avanti for the west coast line. Normally, you have to travel on the line that you bought a ticket for, but if that’s disrupted you can use the other one. If everyone went on the faster east coast route then it would be overloaded, so it’s reasonable to spread the passengers across both east and west coast lines. It would be unreasonable if Edinburgh passengers tried to cut back to the east using the Settle or Transpennine lines, as then I would never get a seat. Randomusername222

If the people making that announcement can’t tell you, how are you supposed to know?…
